drills.instructions: Start close to the basket with the ball in front of the body. Slowly lift the shooting elbow and ball up toward eye level, then finish the shot. The ball should move up cleanly, not around the side of the head. Rebound, reset, repeat. Do 8-10 makes.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor ball path, slow release, low shot consistency, or side-swing mechanics. Assign if the player brings the ball around the hip, across the face, or behind the head before shooting. Do the lift without shooting first.
drills.statistic: A cleaner ball path makes the shot easier to repeat. Beginners need a simple lift pattern before quick releases or movement shots.
drills.safety: Keep the motion smooth. Do not force the shoulder.

drills.name: Seams-to-Rim Shot Prep
drills.reps_target: reps, keep it quick
drills.instructions: Start close to the basket. Before every shot, quickly turn the ball so the shooting hand feels the seams in a comfortable spot. Set the hand, shoot, hold the finish. Rebound, reset the hand placement, repeat. Do not take too long — the goal is awareness, not a slow routine.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor hand placement, inconsistent grip, low release feel, or weak shooting touch. Assign if the hand is on a different part of the ball every shot or the ball comes off unevenly. Let the player shoot without seam focus if it causes overthinking.
drills.statistic: Players do not need a perfect grip every time, but beginners benefit from learning what a clean hand placement feels like. It helps the ball leave the hand more consistently.
drills.safety: Keep the routine short. Do not make the player freeze before every shot.

drills.name: Catch Ready Hands Shot
drills.reps_target: reps, show hands before each pass
drills.instructions: A passer stands close. Start with hands up and ready before the pass. The passer gives a soft pass. Catch with two hands, bring the ball into shooting motion, and shoot from beginner range. Rebound or pass back, repeat. Show hands before every pass.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low catch readiness, poor hand target, slow shot prep, or low catch-and-shoot control. Assign if the player waits for the ball to arrive before getting hands ready. Use slower passes if catching is hard.
drills.statistic: A shot starts before the catch. Ready hands help the player catch clean and shoot in rhythm instead of fighting the ball.
drills.safety: Pass to the hands, not the face. Keep the pass soft.

drills.name: Pass Back Shot Prep
drills.reps_target: 8 makes per spot, then switch sides
drills.instructions: Start at a short shooting spot with a partner. Pass to the partner, immediately get the feet and hands ready, catch the return pass, and shoot. Rebound or rotate. The key is not to relax after passing. Do 8 makes from one spot, then switch sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low pass-and-ready score, slow catch prep, poor shooting rhythm, or low team-offense awareness. Assign if the player passes and stands flat-footed instead of preparing for the return. Stand closer if the return pass is hard to handle.
drills.statistic: Players often get open shots after moving the ball. Passing and getting ready again teaches a simple team shooting habit.
drills.safety: Use controlled passes. Keep spacing clear.

drills.name: Lift From Corner Shot
drills.reps_target: reps both corners
drills.instructions: Start in the corner without shooting from deep. Move up a few steps toward the wing, catch a pass or pick up the ball from a coach, set the feet, and shoot from beginner range. Move under control and do not drift sideways on the shot. Reps from both corners.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low relocation shooting, poor foot control, weak catch balance, or low corner-to-wing awareness. Assign if the player stands in the corner and does not know how to move into a shot. Walk the lift first without shooting.
drills.statistic: Relocation shooting helps players learn how to move into open space. Beginners should start with short, controlled lifts before game-speed movement.
drills.safety: No sprinting. Keep the shot inside the player’s range.

drills.name: Drift Stop Shot
drills.reps_target: reps both directions
drills.instructions: Start a few steps from a short shooting spot. Jog or slide lightly into the spot, stop the body completely, then shoot. Coach watches for continued drift. Only count makes where the body stops first. Do both directions.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor drift control, weak shooting balance, low catch control, or moving-body misses. Assign if the player catches and shoots while falling left, right, forward, or backward. Walk into the spot before jogging.
drills.statistic: Drifting changes the shot line and makes the shot harder to repeat. Stopping before the shot builds better balance.
drills.safety: No hard stops. Land and stop softly.

drills.name: Backpedal Into Shot
drills.reps_target: reps, short distance
drills.instructions: Start a few feet closer to the basket than the shooting spot. Backpedal two small steps to the spot, stop with balance, and shoot — do not fall backward on the shot. Rebound, reset, repeat. Keep the distance short.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor backward balance, weak foot control, low shooting stability, or rushed movement shots. Assign if the player moves backward and shoots while leaning away from the rim. Use one backpedal step first.
drills.statistic: Players often move away from pressure before catching or shooting. This teaches the athlete to regain balance before shooting.
drills.safety: No fast backpedaling. Check space behind the player.

drills.name: Pass Fake to Shot
drills.reps_target: reps both sides
drills.instructions: Start at a short shooting spot with the ball. Give a small pass fake to the side, bring the ball back under control, set the feet, and shoot. The fake should be short and realistic, not a huge swing. Rebound, reset, repeat both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low shot patience, weak fake control, poor balance after fake, or low decision confidence. Assign if the player catches and rushes shots without reading the defense. Practice the pass fake without shooting first.
drills.statistic: A pass fake can create a cleaner shot if the player stays balanced. Beginners learn that a fake only works if they can still shoot under control after it.
drills.safety: No defender needed. Keep the fake small.

drills.name: Shot Fake Reset Jumper
drills.reps_target: reps, no defender
drills.instructions: Start at a short shooting spot. Give a small shot fake by lifting the ball and eyes, then bring the ball back to shooting control without moving the pivot foot. After the fake, shoot with balance. Rebound, reset, repeat. No defender yet.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor shot-fake control, rushed shooting, travel risk, or low balance after fake. Assign if the player jumps on the fake, travels after faking, or cannot shoot after resetting. Practice fake-and-hold without shooting first.
drills.statistic: A shot fake should keep the player in control. This teaches patience and legal footwork before adding live defense.
drills.safety: Keep both feet controlled. No jumping into defenders.

drills.name: One-Dribble Pull-Up Right
drills.reps_target: reps from same spot
drills.instructions: Start at beginner midrange with the ball. Take one controlled dribble to the right, gather the ball, stop on balance, and shoot. Rebound and reset at the same spot. Focus on dribble, gather, balance, shoot — not speed.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low off-dribble shooting, poor gather balance, weak right-hand control, or rushed pull-up form. Assign if the player can shoot standing still but loses form after one dribble. Use shorter distance if they have to throw the shot.
drills.statistic: Off-the-dribble shooting is a different skill than spot shooting. A one-dribble pull-up gives beginners a simple way to learn the timing without advanced moves.
drills.safety: No hard stop. Keep the dribble slow until balance improves.

drills.name: One-Dribble Pull-Up Left
drills.reps_target: 6 makes
drills.instructions: Start at beginner midrange with the ball. Take one controlled dribble to the left, gather with two hands, stop balanced, and shoot. Rebound and reset. Go slow enough to keep the ball under control. Do 6 makes.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low weak-side pull-up control, poor gather, weak left-hand dribble, or off-balance shooting. Assign if the player avoids dribbling left into shots or loses form after a left-hand dribble. Use a closer shot or no shot if the gather is poor.
drills.statistic: Players need to shoot after moving both directions. Left-side pull-up work keeps the player from becoming one-sided.
drills.safety: Controlled speed only. Stop if the player twists the knee or lands off balance.

drills.name: Dribble Stop Set Shot
drills.reps_target: reps from different short spots
drills.instructions: Start a few steps from a short shooting spot. Take two slow dribbles to the spot, stop fully, set the base, and shoot. The stop must happen before the shot starts. Rebound and repeat from different short spots.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor dribble-to-shot control, rushed shot prep, weak stopping balance, or low shot consistency. Assign if the player dribbles into a shot while still moving or falling forward. Use one slow dribble first.
drills.statistic: Beginners often blend the dribble and shot too fast. Stopping first teaches balance and control before harder pull-up work.
drills.safety: No speed. Stop safely before shooting.

drills.name: Pound Dribble Lift Shot
drills.reps_target: reps both hands
drills.instructions: Start at a short shooting spot. Take one strong pound dribble, catch the ball back into the hands, lift into the shot, and shoot. The dribble should be controlled and close to the body. Rebound, reset, repeat. Do both right- and left-hand pound dribbles.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low dribble rhythm, poor shot timing, weak gather control, or stiff set-shot mechanics. Assign if the player’s shot looks stiff from a standstill but better with a simple rhythm. Use dribble-stop set shot first if they cannot gather cleanly.
drills.statistic: Some players shoot better when the dribble gives them rhythm. This teaches that rhythm while keeping the movement simple.
drills.safety: Keep the dribble low and controlled. No rushed pull-ups yet.

drills.name: Partner Call Shot
drills.reps_target: reps, react to the call
drills.instructions: Stand at a short shooting spot with a partner or coach holding the ball. The coach says "ready," then passes and calls "shoot." Catch, set the body, and shoot — do not panic on the call. Rebound or pass back, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low shot readiness, poor reaction focus, rushed catch-and-shoot, or low communication confidence. Assign if the player looks surprised by passes or hurries shots under simple pressure. Use slower calls and softer passes first.
drills.statistic: Players need to be ready before the ball arrives. A simple call-and-pass setup adds focus without turning it into a pressure drill.
drills.safety: No hard passes. Keep the shot close and controlled.

drills.name: Shot Clock Countdown Short Shot
drills.reps_target: 8-10 reps from close range
drills.instructions: Start at a short shooting spot. The coach counts down from 3 out loud. Get the shot off before the count ends, but the shot still has to be balanced. If you rush and lose form, the rep does not count. Do 8-10 reps from close range.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low pressure control, rushed shooting, slow shot prep, or low confidence. Assign if the player panics when they feel time pressure. Count down from 5 if they need more time.
drills.statistic: Pressure should be added slowly. A short countdown gives beginners a small challenge while keeping the shot simple and close.
drills.safety: Do not rush into bad landings. Form still comes first.

drills.name: Partner Contest Hand Shot
drills.reps_target: reps, no contact
drills.instructions: Start at a short spot. A partner stands a safe distance away with one hand up, not touching the shooter. Catch or start with the ball, shoot over the visual hand, and hold the finish. The partner stays still and does not jump into the shooter. Rebound, reset, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low visual focus, poor contest confidence, rushed release, or low shot discipline. Assign if the player changes form every time a hand is near them. Use a cone or raised foam stick instead of a person.
drills.statistic: Players need to keep their eyes and form steady with a closeout hand nearby — a safe first step before live contests.
drills.safety: No body contact. Defender must not step into the shooter’s landing space.

drills.name: Follow Your Shot Midrange
drills.reps_target: 10 reps from one spot
drills.instructions: Shoot from beginner midrange. After the shot leaves the hand, follow the shot toward the rim under control, grab the rebound, and return to the same spot. Do not sprint wildly or crash into others. Shoot 10 reps from one spot.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low rebound awareness, poor follow-shot habit, low shooting focus, or low effort after release. Assign if the player shoots and immediately walks away or watches the ball. Use walking follow only in crowded gyms.
drills.statistic: Players should learn the rep does not end when the ball leaves the hand. Following the shot builds effort and rebound awareness.
drills.safety: No crashing into other players. Move under control.

drills.name: Short Relocate After Pass Shot
drills.reps_target: reps both sides
drills.instructions: Start on the wing with a partner. Pass to the partner, slide or step a few feet to a new short shooting spot, show hands, catch the return pass, and shoot. Keep the movement small and controlled. Rebound, reset, repeat both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low relocation habit, poor off-ball movement, weak catch balance, or low team shooting awareness. Assign if the player passes and stays frozen instead of moving to open space. Walk the relocation first without shooting.
drills.statistic: Moving after the pass creates open shots. This teaches that habit without requiring a full offensive action.
drills.safety: Keep movement short. Do not drift into other players.

drills.name: Trail Spot-Up Shot
drills.reps_target: reps, jog speed
drills.instructions: Start near half court or the top area. Jog into the front court as a trailer, stop at a short shooting spot near the top or slot, catch a pass, and shoot. Stop before shooting and do not drift forward. Rebound, reset, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low transition shooting awareness, poor stop balance, weak catch-and-shoot control, or low trail spacing. Assign if the player runs down the floor and crowds the paint instead of finding a shooting spot. Start closer to the hoop and jog slowly.
drills.statistic: Transition spacing creates open shots. Trail spot-up work helps beginners learn where to arrive and how to shoot under control.
drills.safety: Jog speed first. No crowded lanes or rushed shots.

drills.name: Baseline Lift Short Shot
drills.reps_target: reps both baselines
drills.instructions: Start near the baseline or short corner. Lift a few steps up toward the wing, catch a pass or pick up the ball, stop balanced, and shoot from beginner range. Do not run all the way to the three-point line. Rebound, reset, repeat both baselines.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low baseline movement, poor relocation balance, weak short shot confidence, or low off-ball shooting awareness. Assign if the player stays stuck on the baseline and does not know how to lift into open space. Walk the lift first and shoot closer.
drills.statistic: Simple lifts are common in spacing. Beginners can learn the movement without needing deep range or advanced reads.
drills.safety: Keep the shot close. No sprinting into the catch.

drills.name: Noodle Arc Shot
drills.reps_target: 6-8 makes, rest, repeat
drills.instructions: A coach stands a few feet in front and holds a pool noodle straight up, safely away from the body. Start close to the basket. Shoot the ball over the noodle with a soft arc and hold the finish. Rebound, reset, repeat. The goal is a soft shot that clears the noodle and still lands near the rim — not high for no reason. Do 6-8 makes, rest, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low arc, hard misses, poor shot softness, or low touch. Assign if the shot hits the front rim hard, has very little arc, or looks pushed straight forward. Remove the noodle if the player starts throwing the ball instead of shooting it.
drills.statistic: Youth resources teach arc, touch, and age-appropriate distance before deeper shooting. A soft visual obstacle helps the player feel a higher shot path without a defender or pressure.
drills.safety: The noodle must stay away from the shooter. No jumping into the coach.

drills.name: Chair Sit-to-Stand Shot
drills.reps_target: 6-8 clean makes
drills.instructions: Sit lightly on the front edge of a chair or bench, close to the basket, holding the ball in shooting position. Stand up under control and shoot as the body comes up — no jump, no leaning back, no throwing. Rebound, sit back down, reset, repeat. Do 6-8 clean makes.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor leg rhythm, arm-heavy shot, weak shot power, or low body control. Assign if the player shoots with stiff legs or throws the ball from the chest or shoulder. Do standing rhythm shots if the chair setup is not safe.
drills.statistic: Good youth shooting starts with safe, repeatable mechanics. This teaches leg timing with very low impact and no jump volume.
drills.safety: Use a stable chair. No falling backward. Coach should watch the setup.

drills.name: Color Cone Shot Call
drills.reps_target: reps, slow movement first
drills.instructions: Place three colored cones around beginner range (short wing, short slot, short corner). Start in the middle with the ball or receive a pass. The coach calls a color. Move to that cone, stop balanced, and shoot from that spot. Rebound and reset. Keep the movement slow at first.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low reaction focus, poor court awareness, weak shot balance, or low spot recognition. Assign if the player gets confused moving between spots or rushes when a coach calls a direction. Use two cones instead of three for younger players.
drills.statistic: Decision-based shooting should start simple. Color calls give young players a light reaction task while keeping the shot short and controlled.
drills.safety: No sprinting between cones. Stop balanced before shooting.

drills.name: Handoff Set Shot
drills.reps_target: reps both sides
drills.instructions: A coach or teammate stands near the wing or slot holding the ball. Walk toward the handoff, take the ball with two hands, take one small step into balance, and shoot from beginner range. Do not rush or drift after taking the ball. Rebound, reset, repeat both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low handoff timing, poor shot prep after handoff, weak catch control, or low team shooting awareness. Assign if the player takes a handoff and looks unsure, fumbles, or cannot get balanced before shooting. Walk the exchange without shooting first.
drills.statistic: Handoffs are common in youth offense. This teaches the exchange and shot prep without defenders, screens, or speed.
drills.safety: No screens or contact. Keep the exchange slow and clean.

drills.name: Cone Curl Short Shot
drills.reps_target: reps both sides
drills.instructions: Place a cone near the elbow or short wing as a screen marker. Start a few steps away. Jog slowly around the cone, curl toward the basket, catch a pass or pick up the ball, set the feet, and shoot from short range. Do not drift sideways. Reps from both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low curl footwork, poor catch balance, weak movement shooting, or low shot readiness. Assign if the player moves around a screen marker but cannot stop and shoot under control. Walk the curl first without shooting.
drills.statistic: Movement shooting is easier to learn with a cone before a live screen. The player gets the footwork and balance first.
drills.safety: No live screens. Keep the curl slow and controlled.

drills.name: Cone Flare Short Shot
drills.reps_target: reps both sides
drills.instructions: Place a cone near the wing as a screen marker. Start near the lane line. Move away from the basket at an angle, like flaring to open space. Catch a pass, stop with balance, and shoot from beginner range. Keep the shot short enough for clean form. Reps from both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low flare awareness, poor foot control, weak catch-and-shoot balance, or low off-ball shooting confidence. Assign if the player only moves toward the ball and does not understand moving into open shooting space. Walk the flare angle first.
drills.statistic: A flare movement teaches spacing and balance. Beginners should learn the movement at short range before adding speed or deeper shots.
drills.safety: No sprinting. No deep shots. Keep the movement small and safe.

drills.name: Extra Pass Short Shot
drills.reps_target: rotate after each rep
drills.instructions: Use three players, or two players and a coach. Player 1 passes to Player 2. Player 2 makes one more pass to Player 3. Player 3 catches, sets the feet, and shoots from beginner range. Rotate after each rep. The shooter should be ready before the ball arrives, not surprised by it.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low extra-pass awareness, poor catch readiness, weak team shooting rhythm, or low shot prep. Assign if the player watches passes instead of getting ready to shoot. Use two-player passing first if three-player timing is too hard.
drills.statistic: Youth resources teach team habits along with skill work. Extra-pass shooting teaches spacing, readiness, and simple decision habits without live defense.
drills.safety: Use soft passes. Keep all shots inside beginner range.

drills.name: Skip Pass Catch Shot
drills.reps_target: reps, controlled passes
drills.instructions: A passer stands on one side of the court. The shooter stands at a short spot on the opposite side, inside beginner range. The passer throws a safe skip pass. Show hands early, catch, set the feet, and shoot. Rebound or rotate. Keep the pass controlled, not a hard throw.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low skip-pass catch control, poor hand readiness, weak shot prep, or low cross-court awareness. Assign if the player gets surprised by passes from across the court or catches off balance. Shorten the pass distance if catching is hard.
drills.statistic: Game shots often come from different pass angles. Skip-pass shooting teaches players to prepare early and organize the feet before shooting.
drills.safety: No hard passes to young players. Keep the distance age-appropriate.

drills.name: High Catch Set Shot
drills.reps_target: reps, soft tosses
drills.instructions: A coach stands close and tosses the ball slightly above the chest or shoulder level. Catch with two hands, bring the ball down only to the shooting pocket, and shoot from short range. Do not drop the ball to the waist. Reset and repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor high-catch control, slow shot prep, low hand strength, or weak catch-and-shoot rhythm. Assign if the player catches high passes awkwardly, drops the ball too low, or rushes the shot. Use chest-level passes first if high catches are too hard.
drills.statistic: Players do not always receive perfect passes. Catching a high pass and still shooting under control builds useful game readiness.
drills.safety: No passes near the face. Keep throws soft and controlled.

drills.name: Low Catch Set Shot
drills.reps_target: reps from short range
drills.instructions: A coach gives a soft low pass near the knees or waist. Bend the knees, catch with two hands, bring the ball up to the shooting pocket, set the feet, and shoot. Do not bend only at the waist. Reset and repeat from short range.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low-catch control, poor shot prep, weak lower-body position, or low catch-and-shoot confidence. Assign if the player fumbles low passes or shoots before getting balanced. Start with waist-level passes before knee-level passes.
drills.statistic: Bad passes happen in games. A beginner shooter needs to catch low, use the legs, and still get into a clean shot.
drills.safety: Bend the knees. Do not round the back or reach wildly.

drills.name: Inside-Out Pass Shot
drills.reps_target: rotate or reset after each rep
drills.instructions: A passer starts in the paint or short post area. The shooter starts at a short wing or short corner spot. The passer kicks the ball out. Catch, get balanced, and shoot from beginner range. Rotate or reset. The shooter should be ready before the pass leaves the paint.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low inside-out awareness, poor catch readiness, weak spot shooting rhythm, or low team shooting confidence. Assign if the player does not get ready when a teammate drives or posts. Use a shorter pass if timing is hard.
drills.statistic: Inside-out passes create clean shots because the defense often collapses toward the paint. Beginners can learn the simple habit without advanced reads.
drills.safety: No live defense or contact in the paint. Keep passes controlled.

drills.name: Short Roll Pop Shot
drills.reps_target: reps, stop before shooting
drills.instructions: Start near the elbow or slot. Take two controlled steps toward the paint like rolling, then stop at beginner midrange. A passer gives the ball. Catch, set the feet, and shoot. Stop before shooting and stay inside your range.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low short-roll awareness, poor stop balance, weak catch-and-shoot control, or low paint-area shooting confidence. Assign if the player rolls too deep every time or cannot stop and shoot with balance. Walk the movement first without shooting.
drills.statistic: Not every roll has to end at the rim. A short roll pop teaches the player to stop in space and take a controlled short shot.
drills.safety: No screens, no contact, no speed. Stop balanced first.

drills.name: Pin-Down Walk-Up Shot
drills.reps_target: reps both sides
drills.instructions: Place a cone near the lane as the screen marker. Start low near the baseline. Walk or jog up around the cone, catch a pass near beginner range, set the feet, and shoot. Come around tight but controlled. Rebound, reset, repeat both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low screen-movement awareness, poor catch balance, weak shot prep, or low off-ball shooting. Assign if the player does not know how to come off a screen marker into a shot. Walk the route without the ball first.
drills.statistic: Screen shooting should be taught without contact first. A cone pin-down lets the player learn the path, catch, and balance before live action.
drills.safety: No live screen contact. Keep speed controlled.

drills.name: Baseline Drift Short Shot
drills.reps_target: reps both baselines
drills.instructions: Start near the short corner. A coach cues "drift." Slide or jog a few steps along the baseline to a new short spot. Catch the pass, stop, and shoot. Keep the shot close enough for good form. Do both baselines.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low baseline spacing, poor catch balance, weak relocation shooting, or low drive-and-kick awareness. Assign if the player stands still when a teammate drives baseline. Walk the drift before adding the pass.
drills.statistic: Baseline drift is a simple spacing habit. Beginners can learn the movement at short range before deeper corner shooting.
drills.safety: Watch the baseline boundary. No sprinting into the shot.

drills.name: Nail Catch Short Shot
drills.reps_target: reps
drills.instructions: Start at the nail, the middle area around the free throw line. A passer gives the ball. Catch, set the feet, and shoot from beginner range. Keep the body straight and do not fade left or right. Rebound and repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low nail-area shooting, poor middle-floor balance, weak catch-and-shoot control, or low short-shot confidence. Assign if the player catches in the middle and rushes or turns sideways before shooting. Move closer if the free throw line area is too far.
drills.statistic: The nail is a useful teaching spot because it gives a straight view of the rim and connects passing, spacing, and short shooting.
drills.safety: Stay inside the player’s real range. No forced distance.

drills.name: Short Corner Lift Catch Shot
drills.reps_target: reps both sides
drills.instructions: Start in the short corner. Lift up a few steps toward the wing, catch a pass, set the feet, and shoot from beginner range. Do not drift while shooting. Rebound, reset, repeat both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low short-corner awareness, poor relocation balance, weak catch-and-shoot control, or low spot spacing. Assign if the player stays buried near the baseline and does not move into a passing window. Walk the lift first without a shot.
drills.statistic: Short corner lifts are simple and useful for spacing. For beginners, the shot must stay close enough to keep the form clean.
drills.safety: Keep movement small. No deep corner shots.

drills.name: Slot Fill Catch Shot
drills.reps_target: reps both sides
drills.instructions: Start on the wing. The coach or passer cues the player to fill up to the slot. Move to the slot, show hands, catch the pass, set the feet, and shoot from beginner range. Rebound and reset. Do both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low fill movement, poor shot readiness, weak catch balance, or low spacing awareness. Assign if the player does not understand moving into open perimeter spots. Use a closer slot spot if shooting range is limited.
drills.statistic: Filling open space is one of the first spacing habits young players learn. This connects that movement to a short, controlled shot.
drills.safety: No rushing or drifting. Stop before shooting.

drills.name: Corner Replace Short Shot
drills.reps_target: reps both corners
drills.instructions: A cone marks the wing spot and another marks the corner spot. Start at the corner. On the coach cue, move up to replace the wing spot, catch the pass, and shoot from beginner range. Arrive balanced and ready. Reset and repeat both corners.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low replace movement, poor catch readiness, weak spot awareness, or low off-ball shooting habits. Assign if the player stands still after a teammate leaves a spot. Walk the replace movement first.
drills.statistic: Replace movement is a simple way to keep spacing. Beginners can learn it before more advanced motion offense concepts.
drills.safety: Keep the movement short and the shot close.

drills.name: Quick Feet Set Shot
drills.reps_target: reps
drills.instructions: Start a few feet from a short shooting spot. Do quick feet in place for 3 seconds. On the coach cue, step to the shooting spot, stop, and shoot. Do not shoot while bouncing or leaning. Rebound, reset, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor foot control, weak balance after movement, rushed shots, or low shot readiness. Assign if the player gets excited after quick feet and shoots off balance. Use slower feet or shorter reps for younger players.
drills.statistic: Game shots often happen after movement. This teaches the player to calm the body before the ball goes up.
drills.safety: No hard jumping or sprinting. Stop balanced before shooting.

drills.name: Coach Hand Signal Shot
drills.reps_target: reps, keep it slow
drills.instructions: Start at a short shooting spot with the ball. A coach stands in front or to the side and gives one of two hand signals: one means shoot, the other means hold and reset. On the shoot signal, set the feet and shoot. On the hold signal, stay balanced and do not shoot. Keep it simple and slow.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low visual focus, rushed shot decisions, poor patience, or low coach-cue response. Assign if the player shoots every time they touch the ball without looking or thinking. Use only one signal first if the player gets confused.
drills.statistic: Decision-making can start with simple cues. This gives beginners a safe way to practice seeing before shooting without adding defenders.
drills.safety: No pressure or yelling. Keep the player calm and balanced.

drills.name: Clean Range Finder
drills.reps_target: step back until form breaks, mark last clean spot
drills.instructions: Start very close to the basket and take short shots with normal form. If the player can make shots without throwing, leaning, or pushing with two hands, take one small step back. Once the player forces the ball, drops the form, or misses badly because of distance, stop and mark the last clean spot — that is the player’s current form range.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for shooting strength, age-appropriate range, form consistency, and shot confidence. Assign if the player throws from the chest, leans back, loses guide-hand control, or cannot reach the rim without changing form. Use a lower rim or smaller ball for younger players if regulation forces bad form. Do not move the player beyond clean range just because they are talented.
drills.statistic: Young players often miss because the shot is too far for their strength, not effort. Finding the real form range protects mechanics and gives the app a better distance ceiling.
drills.safety: Stop as soon as the player starts throwing or leaning. Do not reward forced range.

drills.name: Lower-Rim Smooth Shot
drills.reps_target: 8-10 makes close, rest, repeat
drills.instructions: Set the rim lower if the gym allows. Start close to the basket with the right ball size for the player’s age. Shoot with normal form, relaxed shoulders, and a smooth release. Watch for clean motion, not deep range. Make 8-10 from close range, rest, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low shooting strength, poor regulation-rim mechanics, low confidence, or forced two-hand push. Assign if the shot looks clean on a lower rim but breaks down on a regulation rim. Use close-range regulation shots only if no lower rim is available.
drills.statistic: A lower rim helps younger players practice the right motion instead of building bad habits just to reach the basket. The goal is clean reps that match the athlete’s strength.
drills.safety: Use a stable adjustable rim. Do not let players hang on the rim or crowd underneath.

drills.name: Smaller Ball Smooth Release
drills.reps_target: 8-10 clean makes, rest
drills.instructions: Use an age-appropriate ball. Start close to the basket and shoot short, smooth shots. Watch whether the ball comes off the hand cleanly and whether the player can hold it without squeezing or pushing with both hands. After 8-10 clean makes, rest. Do not switch to a bigger ball until the smaller ball looks controlled.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for hand-size limits, poor grip control, weak release, or forced two-hand shooting. Assign if the player cannot control the ball in one hand or it slips during the release. Use close no-shot grip work first if the player cannot hold the ball safely.
drills.statistic: Ball size matters for young shooters. A player who cannot control the ball usually builds a push or side-spin habit. This keeps the tool matched to the athlete.
drills.safety: Do not force a regulation ball if it breaks the player’s form.

drills.name: No-Rim Form Lift
drills.reps_target: 8 slow reps, rest, repeat
drills.instructions: Stand in open space with the ball. Bend the knees slightly, lift the ball along a clean path, finish with the shooting hand toward an imaginary rim, and hold the finish. The ball can stay in the hands or be lightly tossed a few feet up and caught. Do 8 slow reps, rest, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor shooting motion, low strength, rushed release, or bad ball path. Assign if the player’s shot breaks down when a hoop is involved. Use a lighter ball if the player cannot lift the ball smoothly.
drills.statistic: Removing the rim takes pressure off the athlete. The player learns the motion first, then adds the basket once strength and control improve.
drills.safety: Do not throw the ball high. Keep reps slow and controlled.

drills.name: Mirror Shot Shape
drills.reps_target: 5 slow reps, feedback, 5 more
drills.instructions: Stand in front of a mirror, window reflection, or a coach holding a camera. Go through the shooting motion slowly without shooting at a basket. Check the feet, knees, ball path, elbow, and finish. Do 5 slow reps, pause for feedback, then 5 more. Do not rush.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low body awareness, poor shot shape, inconsistent setup, or low form understanding. Assign if the player cannot feel when the shot is off balance or crooked. Use coach demonstration if no mirror is available.
drills.statistic: Beginners often cannot feel form mistakes yet. Visual feedback helps connect coach cues to what the body is actually doing.
drills.safety: Use safe open space. No shooting into glass.

drills.name: Quiet Shoulder Shot
drills.reps_target: 8 makes
drills.instructions: Start very close to the basket. Before shooting, relax the shoulders and take a small breath. Shoot a short shot while keeping the shoulders quiet and the head still. Check if the shoulders jumped up or twisted. Rebound, reset, repeat for 8 makes.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for shoulder tension, poor upper-body control, rushed release, or hard misses. Assign if the player shrugs, twists, or throws the ball from the upper body. Move closer or use a smaller ball if the player tenses up because of distance.
drills.statistic: Tension makes the shot harder to repeat. A relaxed upper body helps the player shoot softer and stay on line.
drills.safety: Stop if shoulder pain appears. Do not add range.

drills.name: Short Rainbow Arc Shot
drills.reps_target: 8 makes close
drills.instructions: Start close to the basket. Shoot the ball like a small rainbow, not a hard pass — let it go up, peak, and come down softly near the rim. Rebound and reset. Do 8 makes from close range.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low arc, poor touch, flat misses, or low shot softness. Assign if the shot hits the front rim hard or looks like a pass. Use a lower rim or smaller ball if the player cannot create arc without throwing.
drills.statistic: Soft arc gives the ball a better chance to drop in. For young players, the drill must stay close so arc does not turn into a forced heave.
drills.safety: Stay close. Do not let the player lean back to get arc.

drills.name: Front-Rim Drop Shot
drills.reps_target: 6-8 soft makes
drills.instructions: Start close to the basket. Shoot so the ball clears the front rim softly and drops in — do not aim hard at the back rim. Rebound, reset, repeat. Count only shots that are soft and controlled. Do 6-8 makes.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor distance control, hard misses, low touch, or front-rim misses. Assign if the player hits the front rim with a flat shot or launches the ball too hard. Move closer if the player cannot clear the front rim softly.
drills.statistic: Good shooters learn distance control. This gives a simple target: clear the front rim with touch instead of throwing the ball.
drills.safety: Keep reps low and close. Do not force power.

drills.name: Back-Rim Soft Touch Shot
drills.reps_target: 6-8 soft makes
drills.instructions: Start close to the basket. Shoot softly toward the back half of the rim — the ball should not fly hard off the back rim. Shoot, check the miss, rebound, reset. Do 6-8 makes or clean soft attempts.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for short misses, low depth control, weak touch, or low confidence from beginner range. Assign if the shots keep hitting the front rim or falling short. Move closer or lower the rim if the player cannot reach softly.
drills.statistic: Some players miss short because they are underpowered or unsure. This teaches depth control without telling the player to throw harder.
drills.safety: Do not push range. The shot must stay smooth.

drills.name: Two-Step Range Step-In
drills.reps_target: 8-10 reps
drills.instructions: Start at a marked beginner spot. If the player can shoot with clean form, take the shot. If it feels too far or the coach sees bad form, take two steps in, reset, and shoot from the closer spot. Rebound and go back to the starting mark. Repeat for 8-10 reps.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor shot selection, forced range, low shooting strength, or low form awareness. Assign if the player keeps shooting from too far even when mechanics break down. Start closer if the first spot is already too far.
drills.statistic: Shot selection starts with knowing your range. Young players need permission to move in when form breaks down.
drills.safety: Never punish a player for stepping closer. Clean form is the win.

drills.name: Soft Ball Touch Shot
drills.reps_target: 8-10 clean reps, rest
drills.instructions: Use a soft training ball, foam ball, or lighter basketball if available. Stand close to the basket or a lower hoop and shoot with the same motion as with a real ball. Watch the release, arc, and balance. Do 8-10 clean reps, then rest.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low hand strength, low shot control, poor release, or forced regulation-ball mechanics. Assign if the player cannot shoot a standard ball without pushing or twisting. Use a smaller basketball instead if a soft ball changes the feel too much.
drills.statistic: A lighter ball reduces the strength barrier so the player can learn touch and release — a lower-load rung, not a permanent replacement for a normal basketball.
drills.safety: Use a safe ball. Do not throw hard indoors.

drills.name: Partner Form Toss to Hands
drills.reps_target: 8 clean shots
drills.instructions: A passer stands close and tosses the ball softly to the player’s hands. Catch, pause for balance, then shoot from close range. The pass should be easy enough to catch without panic. Get the ball and pass it back. Do 8 clean shots.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low catch strength, poor shot prep, weak hand control, or rushed catch-and-shoot mechanics. Assign if the player bobbles normal passes before shooting. Use a smaller or lighter ball if catching is still hard.
drills.statistic: Young players need passes that match their hand strength. If every pass is too hard, the shot rep breaks before it starts.
drills.safety: Pass softly to the hands. No chest-high rockets.

drills.name: Close Chair Balance Shot
drills.reps_target: 6-8 makes
drills.instructions: Place a chair a safe distance beside the player, not in front of the feet. Stand close to the basket. Before shooting, lightly touch the chair with the off hand for balance, then let go and shoot. The chair is only a reminder. Rebound, reset, repeat. Do 6-8 makes.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor shooting balance, body sway, weak base, or low posture control. Assign if the player cannot stay still during a short shot. Remove the chair if the player leans on it too much.
drills.statistic: Some beginners need a physical reminder to feel balance. The drill keeps the load low and the shot close while teaching body control.
drills.safety: Use a stable chair and keep it away from the feet. Do not let the player trip.

drills.name: Eyes-Lift Shot
drills.reps_target: reps, eyes to rim before motion
drills.instructions: Start close to the basket with the ball. Before each shot, say "eyes" and look at the rim for one full second, then shoot with balance. Rebound and reset. The eyes must reach the rim before the shooting motion starts.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor visual focus, rushed shot prep, low target awareness, or inconsistent aim. Assign if the player watches the ball while shooting or looks at the rim too late. Use no-shot "eyes only" reps first if the player rushes.
drills.statistic: A shooter needs to see the target before the ball leaves the hand. This simple cue helps beginners slow down and aim with purpose.
drills.safety: Keep the shot close. No pressure.

drills.name: Quiet Feet Shot
drills.reps_target: 8 clean makes (feet must stay still)
drills.instructions: Start at a close shooting spot. The feet must stay quiet from the start of the shot until the ball leaves the hand. If the feet move, the rep does not count. Shoot, hold balance, rebound, repeat. Do 8 clean makes.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for foot movement, poor base stability, rushed shooting, or inconsistent shot balance. Assign if the player shuffles, steps, or bounces during short set shots. Move closer if the feet move because the shot is too far.
drills.statistic: A stable base helps the shot repeat. Beginners often move their feet because they are off balance or shooting outside their strength range.
drills.safety: Do not freeze the knees. Keep a comfortable bend.

drills.name: Small Step-In Shot
drills.reps_target: reps both sides
drills.instructions: Start one small step behind a close shooting spot. Step in with the shooting-side foot, bring the other foot into balance, and shoot. Keep the step small and quiet. Rebound and repeat from both sides. Keep the spot close enough for good form.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor step-in control, low shooting rhythm, weak balance, or slow shot prep. Assign if the player needs rhythm but a hop or faster footwork is too much. Use stationary shooting if stepping causes form breakdown.
drills.statistic: A small step-in is a lower-impact way to build rhythm — easier than faster movement shooting and safer for young players.
drills.safety: No jump needed. Keep the step small.

drills.name: Short Pass Catch Pause Shoot
drills.reps_target: 8 makes
drills.instructions: A passer stands close and gives a soft pass. Catch the ball, pause for one second, check the feet, then shoot from close range. The pause is part of the drill. Rebound or pass back and repeat. Do 8 makes.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor catch control, rushed shot prep, weak balance, or low hand strength. Assign if the player catches and immediately throws the ball before getting set. Use an even softer pass or smaller ball if catching is hard.
drills.statistic: Some young players need a pause before rhythm. Rushing before they are strong or coordinated enough can build bad mechanics.
drills.safety: Soft passes only. Give the player time to set.

drills.name: Soft Touch Backboard Shot
drills.reps_target: reps both sides
drills.instructions: Start a few feet from the basket at a short angle. Set the feet, look at a soft spot on the glass, and shoot a short bank-style shot with light touch from a set position (not a drive). Rebound, reset, repeat both sides. Stay close enough to avoid throwing.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor glass touch, hard short shots, low angle control, or weak short-range accuracy. Assign if the player can make straight shots but struggles with short angled shots. Move closer or lower the rim if the player cannot shoot softly.
drills.statistic: Short glass shots teach angle, touch, and depth — another safe close-range shot without adding speed or contact.
drills.safety: No drifting or jumping into other players. Keep it close.

drills.name: Wrist-Friendly Push Range Check
drills.reps_target: 5 slow shots, check for pain
drills.instructions: Start very close to the basket. Shoot 5 slow shots with normal form. After each, the coach asks if the wrist, elbow, or shoulder feels okay. If the player feels pain or has to push hard, move closer, use a smaller ball, or stop shooting for the day. The drill is about finding a safe shooting setup.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for pain monitoring, shooting strength, wrist control, and safe range selection. Assign if the player says shooting hurts, shakes the wrist after shots, or visibly forces the ball. Do not continue if pain is present.
drills.statistic: Pain and forced mechanics are warning signs. Young players should build shooting strength slowly and stay within a pain-free range.
drills.safety: Pain stops the drill. Do not coach through wrist, elbow, or shoulder pain.

drills.name: Parent-Range Spot Shot
drills.reps_target: 10 shots from one marked spot
drills.instructions: A parent or coach helps the player find one close spot where they can shoot with clean form. Mark it with tape, chalk, or a cone. Shoot 10 shots from that spot only. If form stays clean, keep that spot for the week; if form breaks, move it closer. The goal is consistent, safe reps.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for home-practice safety, age-appropriate range, low confidence, or poor shot selection. Assign if the player practices deep shots at home and builds bad habits. Use a lower rim or smaller ball if clean form is not possible.
drills.statistic: Kids often copy older players and shoot from too far away. A marked parent-range spot keeps practice productive and protects the shot.
drills.safety: No deep shots during this drill. Stay at the marked clean-form spot.

drills.name: Ball Tap Finger Warm-Up
drills.reps_target: 10-15s, rest, repeat
drills.instructions: Stand in place with a basketball. Tap the ball quickly but lightly between both hands at chest height — the ball moves hand to hand without being thrown high. Start with 10-15 seconds, rest, repeat. Younger players use a smaller ball and slower taps.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low hand comfort, poor ball feel, weak finger control, or low catching confidence. Assign if the player fumbles easy catches, slaps the ball, or looks uncomfortable holding it. Use a smaller or lighter ball if the player cannot control the tap.
drills.statistic: Ball familiarity comes before passing speed. Young players need to feel the ball in the hands before they can catch and pass with confidence.
drills.safety: Do not tap near the face. Keep the ball at chest height or lower.

drills.name: Around-the-Waist Ball Wrap
drills.reps_target: 5 circles each direction
drills.instructions: Stand tall with the ball in both hands. Move the ball around the waist in a circle, passing it from one hand to the other. Go 5 circles one way, then 5 the other. Start slow; keep the body still and move only the ball and hands.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor hand coordination, low ball control, weak grip comfort, or low body awareness. Assign if the player drops the ball during simple hand changes. Use a smaller ball if the hands are too small.
drills.statistic: Basic ball wraps improve comfort and hand coordination before more difficult passing or dribbling — low-impact and safe for younger athletes.
drills.safety: Slow first. Do not let the player twist the back hard to chase the ball.

drills.name: Around-the-Head Ball Wrap
drills.reps_target: 5 circles each direction
drills.instructions: Hold the ball with both hands near the chin. Slowly move it around the head in a circle, passing hand to hand. Go 5 circles one way, then 5 the other. Keep the ball away from the face and move slowly enough to stay in control.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low ball awareness, poor hand transfer, weak shoulder control, or low coordination. Assign if the player loses the ball when moving it around the body. Use around-the-waist wraps first if this feels unsafe.
drills.statistic: Moving the ball around the body builds coordination and comfort — a safer low-load way to improve control before passing under pressure.
drills.safety: Keep the ball away from the face. Stop if shoulder pain appears.

drills.name: Figure-8 Hand-Off
drills.reps_target: 5 clean figure-8s, rest, repeat
drills.instructions: Stand with feet a little wider than shoulder-width, knees slightly bent. Move the ball around one leg, then through the middle and around the other leg — the ball stays in the hands, not dribbled. Start slow, make 5 clean figure-8s, rest, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low coordination, poor hand transfer, weak body control, or low ball comfort. Assign if the player cannot control the ball through simple hand changes. Use the around-the-waist wrap first if the player struggles.
drills.statistic: Figure-8 hand-offs build control without dribbling speed — useful for younger players because the ball stays in the hands.
drills.safety: Keep the knees bent softly. Do not round the back too much.

drills.name: Ball Squeeze and Ready Hands
drills.reps_target: 8-10 reps
drills.instructions: Hold the ball with two hands at chest level. Squeeze the ball for 2 seconds, relax, then move the hands out as a target like ready to catch. A coach gives a soft pass, or simply reset with the ball. Do 8-10 reps. The goal is strong hands, not tight shoulders.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low hand strength, poor ball security, weak catching control, or fumbled passes. Assign if the player catches and the ball slips out or gets knocked loose easily. Use a smaller ball if the player cannot squeeze without strain.
drills.statistic: Some younger athletes miss catches because their hands are not strong or ready yet. This builds a simple grip-and-ready habit before live passing.
drills.safety: Do not over-squeeze if fingers hurt. Use the right ball size.

drills.name: Soft Toss Catch
drills.reps_target: 10 clean catches, rest, repeat
drills.instructions: A coach or partner stands about 4-6 feet away and tosses the ball softly to the chest. Show both hands, catch the ball, pull it in, and say "got it." Then toss it back softly. Do 10 clean catches, rest, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low catch confidence, poor hand readiness, fear of the ball, or weak basic catching. Assign if the player flinches, turns away, or lets easy passes hit the body. Use a foam ball first if the player is afraid of the ball.
drills.statistic: Catching confidence has to come before harder passing drills. Soft tosses lower fear and help the player build trust in the hands.
drills.safety: No hard passes. Pass softly to the chest or hands.

drills.name: Clap Before Catch
drills.reps_target: 10 clean catches
drills.instructions: A coach or partner stands close with the ball. Before the pass, clap once, then open both hands as a target. The passer gives a soft pass. Catch with two hands, pull the ball in, then pass it back. Do 10 clean catches.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor hand readiness, slow reaction, low catch timing, or fumbled passes. Assign if the player waits for the ball to arrive before showing hands. Use soft toss catch first if the player is nervous.
drills.statistic: Young players need simple cues. Clapping before the catch builds awareness that the hands must be ready before the pass arrives.
drills.safety: Pass softly and close. No surprise throws.

drills.name: Catch, Chin, Pivot
drills.reps_target: 5 reps each pivot direction
drills.instructions: Catch a soft pass from a coach or partner. After catching, bring the ball strong to the chin or chest, keep elbows safe and controlled, then make one slow pivot. Pass the ball back. Do 5 reps with a right pivot and 5 with a left pivot.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor ball security, weak pivot control, fumbled catches, or high turnover risk after catches. Assign if the player catches and immediately drops the ball, travels, or turns into pressure. Practice catch-and-chin without pivoting first.
drills.statistic: A catch is not finished until the player controls the ball. Catch-chin-pivot teaches security and calm footwork before the next pass or shot.
drills.safety: Keep elbows controlled. No swinging into other players.

drills.name: Target Hands Partner Pass
drills.reps_target: reps, change target every few
drills.instructions: Two players stand 6-10 feet apart. The receiver shows a clear target with both hands (chest-high or outside-shoulder). The passer throws a controlled pass to that target. The receiver catches, resets, shows a new target, and passes back. Change the target every few reps.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low passing accuracy, poor target recognition, weak catch readiness, or low teammate communication. Assign if the passer throws to random spots or the receiver does not show hands. Shorten the distance or use a smaller ball for younger players.
drills.statistic: Good passes go to a target; good receivers give the passer a target. This drill teaches both sides of the pass.
drills.safety: Use controlled passes. No face passes.

drills.name: Number Call Catch
drills.reps_target: 8-10 reps
drills.instructions: A coach or partner stands close with the ball. Before passing, hold up fingers and call the player’s name. The player says the number out loud, then catches the soft pass. Secure the ball and pass it back. Do 8-10 reps.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low visual focus, poor communication, slow reaction, or weak catch concentration. Assign if the player looks down, misses simple passes, or loses focus when catching. Remove the number call if catching is not safe yet.
drills.statistic: Passing and catching require attention, not just hands. A simple number call adds focus without adding physical pressure.
drills.safety: Soft pass only. Do not distract the player so much that safety drops.

drills.name: Roll Pass to Target
drills.reps_target: 8-10 rolls, then switch spots
drills.instructions: Place a cone, hoop, or floor spot 6-10 feet away. Start with the ball on the floor and roll it toward the target using two hands — straight and controlled. Retrieve the ball and repeat. Do 8-10 rolls, then switch target spots.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low passing strength, poor aim, low confidence, or weak ball control. Assign if the player cannot safely throw or catch yet. Use a lighter ball if the player cannot roll straight.
drills.statistic: Younger players may need a lower-rung passing task before throwing passes. Rolling builds aim, direction, and confidence without stressing the shoulders or fingers.
drills.safety: Keep other players from stepping on rolling balls.

drills.name: Bounce Target Box
drills.reps_target: 10 controlled passes, then switch roles
drills.instructions: Place a tape square, floor dot, or flat marker between passer and receiver. Bounce the ball inside the target box so it rises to the receiver’s hands. Start with the receiver standing still and close. Do 10 controlled passes, then switch roles.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor bounce-pass placement, low passing touch, weak accuracy, or inconsistent pass height. Assign if the player bounces passes too close, too far, or at the receiver’s feet. Move closer or use a larger target box for younger players.
drills.statistic: A bounce pass needs a floor target. Beginners improve faster when they can see where the ball should hit.
drills.safety: Use a flat marker only. No raised objects in the passing lane.

drills.name: Overhead Pass Target
drills.reps_target: 10 reps each
drills.instructions: Two players stand 6-10 feet apart. The passer holds the ball above the forehead with both hands, steps forward, and sends a controlled overhead pass to the receiver’s hands. The receiver catches with two hands and passes back. Keep the pass soft and straight. Do 10 reps each.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for overhead passing control, shoulder strength, target accuracy, or passing variety. Assign if the player only knows chest and bounce passes and is ready for another safe pass type. Avoid if the player lacks shoulder strength or throws from behind the head; ages 7-8 only with a smaller ball and short distance.
drills.statistic: Overhead passing is useful but requires more strength than short chest passing. Younger players should use a smaller ball and short distance.
drills.safety: No hard throws. Stop if shoulder pain appears.

drills.name: Step-to-Target Pass
drills.reps_target: 10 reps
drills.instructions: A player stands with the ball; a partner stands 6-10 feet away. Point the lead foot toward the target, step, and pass with control. After the pass, freeze for one second to check balance. The receiver catches and passes back the same way. Do 10 reps.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor pass footwork, low passing accuracy, weak body control, or arm-only passing. Assign if the player passes while leaning, falling away, or stepping away from the target. Use a shorter distance for younger players.
drills.statistic: Passing accuracy starts with body direction. Stepping to the target helps young players pass with better control and less arm strain.
drills.safety: No lunging. Step short and controlled.

drills.name: Pass and Slide Receive
drills.reps_target: 30s, rest, switch lead role
drills.instructions: Two players face each other. Player A passes to Player B, then slides two steps to the side. Player B passes back to Player A’s new spot. Player A catches, passes back, and slides the other way. Keep the distance short and passes soft. Do 30 seconds, rest, switch lead roles.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low pass-and-move habit, poor receiver readiness, weak lateral control, or low passing rhythm. Assign if the player passes and stands still or cannot catch after small movement. Walk instead of slide for younger or less coordinated players.
drills.statistic: Basketball passing is rarely done while standing still forever. This adds small movement without making the pass too hard.
drills.safety: No fast slides. Keep space clear.

drills.name: Pass, Cut, Fill
drills.reps_target: rotate slowly through both sides
drills.instructions: Use three spots: wing, corner, top. Pass from the wing to a coach/teammate at the top, cut a few steps toward the basket, then fill out to the corner. The coach passes back to the player in the new spot. Catch and pass back. Rotate slowly through both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low spacing awareness, poor pass-and-cut habit, weak catch readiness, or low team-movement understanding. Assign if the player passes and stays frozen or cuts without knowing where to go next. Walk the pattern first without the ball.
drills.statistic: Young players need simple movement patterns. Pass-cut-fill teaches spacing after a pass without adding defenders or complex reads.
drills.safety: Walk first. Keep one ball and clear lanes.

drills.name: Lead Pass to Walking Receiver
drills.reps_target: reps both directions, slow
drills.instructions: A receiver walks slowly from the wing toward the basket or across the court. The passer stands 6-12 feet away and throws a soft pass slightly in front of the receiver. The receiver catches while walking, stops, and passes back. Start slow. Do both directions.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor lead-pass timing, low moving-target accuracy, weak receiver coordination, or low court awareness. Assign if the passer throws behind moving teammates or the receiver has to stop awkwardly. Use stationary target passing first if accuracy is poor.
drills.statistic: Passing to movement is different from passing to a standing teammate. Walking speed lets beginners learn timing without chaos.
drills.safety: Walk only at first. No hard passes.

drills.name: Outlet Turn and Pass
drills.reps_target: reps both sides
drills.instructions: Start near the basket with the ball. Pretend to rebound, bring the ball strong to the chest or chin, pivot toward the sideline, and pass to a teammate or coach near the wing. Keep the pass controlled. Reset and repeat. Work both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor outlet awareness, weak pivot control, low ball security, or rushed passes after rebounds. Assign if the player rebounds and immediately throws the ball into traffic. Practice pivot and ball security before adding the pass; ages 7-8 use shorter distance and a smaller ball.
drills.statistic: A safe outlet pass can prevent turnovers. Beginners need to secure, turn, see, and pass before adding pressure.
drills.safety: No swinging elbows. Keep the pivot slow.

drills.name: Post Feed Target Pass
drills.reps_target: 8 reps, then switch sides
drills.instructions: A receiver stands on the block or short post area and shows a target hand. The passer stands on the wing and makes a controlled pass to the receiver’s target hand, not the defender side. The receiver catches, secures the ball, and passes back. Switch sides after 8 reps.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor post-entry accuracy, low target recognition, weak pass placement, or low teammate awareness. Assign if the player throws post passes too low, too high, or to the wrong side. Use shorter distance and no defender first.
drills.statistic: Post feeds require accuracy and target reading. Beginners should learn the target hand before adding defensive pressure.
drills.safety: No defender contact. Keep passes soft and controlled.

drills.name: Corner Safety Pass
drills.reps_target: reps both corners
drills.instructions: Start in the corner with the ball; a coach stands as a target on the wing or slot. Pivot, protect the ball, and make a controlled safety pass out to the coach. No defender at first. Reset in the corner and repeat. Work both corners.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low corner decision-making, poor pivot control, weak ball security, or high turnover risk. Assign if the player gets trapped in the corner and throws wild passes. Practice the pivot first without passing.
drills.statistic: Corners can feel scary for beginners. A simple safety pass gives the player a calm first option before adding pressure.
drills.safety: No trapping defenders yet. Keep the pass short.

drills.name: Ball Fake to Safe Pass
drills.reps_target: reps both fake directions
drills.instructions: A player stands with the ball; a partner stands 6-10 feet away. Give a small ball fake to one side, keep the feet under control, then pass to the partner’s target hands. The fake should be short and controlled. The partner catches and passes back. Do both fake directions.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low fake control, poor passing decisions, weak balance, or high turnover risk. Assign if the player throws every pass right away without seeing the lane. Use no fake first if the player travels or loses balance.
drills.statistic: A ball fake can open a passing lane, but only if the player stays calm. Beginners need small fakes, not wild swings.
drills.safety: Keep the fake small. No swinging the ball into someone’s face.

drills.name: Circle Pass Names
drills.reps_target: slow, pass to hands not faces
drills.instructions: Players stand in a circle. One player starts with the ball, calls a teammate’s name, makes eye contact, and passes to that player. The receiver catches, secures the ball, calls another name, and passes. Start slow. Pass to hands, not faces.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low communication, poor teammate awareness, weak catch readiness, or low passing confidence. Assign if players pass without looking or do not talk on the court. Use a smaller circle for younger players.
drills.statistic: Passing is also communication. Circle name passing teaches young players to see teammates and talk before the pass.
drills.safety: No hard passes. Make sure players are watching before passing.

drills.name: Two-Ball Partner Roll and Pass
drills.reps_target: slow, switch roll/pass ball
drills.instructions: Two players face each other 6-8 feet apart. Player A rolls one ball on the floor to Player B. At the same time, Player B gives a soft two-hand pass back to Player A with the second ball. Catch or stop each ball, reset, repeat. Go slow. Switch which ball is rolled and which is passed.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low coordination, poor focus, weak timing, or low partner control. Assign if the player can do simple passing but needs better focus and timing. Use one ball only if the player gets overwhelmed; ages 7-8 only if both players are calm.
drills.statistic: Two-ball partner drills add a thinking challenge without contact or speed. This one stays beginner-safe because one ball rolls instead of both being thrown.
drills.safety: Go slow. Watch rolling balls near feet.

drills.name: Passing Lane Window Drill
drills.reps_target: 8 clean passes, then move cones
drills.instructions: Set two cones a few feet apart between passer and receiver to create a passing window. The passer must throw the ball through the window to the receiver’s hands. Start close and use soft passes. After 8 clean passes, move the cones slightly or switch sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low passing-lane awareness, poor accuracy, weak decision-making, or high turnover risk. Assign if the player throws into imaginary defenders or cannot aim through a lane. Make the window wider for younger players.
drills.statistic: Players need to see where the pass can travel safely. A cone window gives beginners a simple visual for passing lanes before live defense.
drills.safety: Use soft passes and flat cones if possible. Keep the window wide at first.

drills.name: Self-Toss Two-Hand Catch
drills.reps_target: 8-10 clean catches
drills.instructions: Stand in place with the ball. Toss it straight up only a few feet, watch it, catch with two hands, and bring it into the chest. Reset after every catch. Start with 8-10 clean catches. Younger players use a smaller or lighter ball if the regular ball is hard to control.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low hand-eye coordination, poor catch confidence, weak ball tracking, or low ball familiarity. Assign if the player flinches, drops easy catches, or struggles catching without pressure. Use a foam ball if the player is afraid of the ball.
drills.statistic: Before a player catches passes from teammates, they need to track and secure the ball safely. A low-load catching rung for younger players.
drills.safety: Keep the toss low. Do not toss near the face.

drills.name: Drop-Bounce Catch
drills.reps_target: 10 clean catches
drills.instructions: Hold the ball at chest height and drop it straight down. After one bounce, catch it with two hands and pull it into the chest. Reset and repeat. Start with 10 clean catches. If the ball bounces too high or fast, use a smaller ball or drop from a lower height.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low reaction timing, poor soft hands, weak ball tracking, or fumbled catches. Assign if the player misjudges bouncing passes or reacts late to the ball. Use self-toss two-hand catch first if tracking is poor.
drills.statistic: Young players often struggle with bounce timing. This isolates the bounce and catch without adding a passer.
drills.safety: Keep the ball in front. Do not chase wild bounces into other players.

drills.name: Meet-the-Pass Catch
drills.reps_target: 8-10 reps, then switch roles
drills.instructions: A passer stands close with the ball. The receiver starts a few steps away with hands ready. On the pass, step toward the ball, catch with two hands, and pull it in strong. Then pass it back softly. Do 8-10 reps, switch roles.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low receiver movement, poor catch strength, weak ball security, or turnover risk. Assign if the player waits flat-footed for passes and gets beat to the ball. Use shorter distance for younger players.
drills.statistic: Receivers help the passer by moving to the ball. This simple habit makes catches safer and reduces lazy-pass turnovers.
drills.safety: Step under control. No lunging or diving.

drills.name: Outside-Shoulder Target Pass
drills.reps_target: reps, switch shoulders
drills.instructions: A receiver stands with one hand showing on the outside shoulder. The passer throws a soft, controlled pass to that outside target hand. The receiver catches, secures, and passes back. After a few reps, switch the target to the other shoulder. Keep the distance short.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low pass placement, poor target recognition, weak teammate awareness, or high turnover risk. Assign if the player passes to the wrong side of the receiver or throws into pressure. Use center target hands first if accuracy is poor; ages 7-8 only with very short distance and soft passes.
drills.statistic: Good passing is not just throwing to a teammate — it is putting the ball where the teammate can catch it safely.
drills.safety: Soft passes only. Keep the target away from the face.

drills.name: Shovel Pass Close Partner
drills.reps_target: 8 reps each side
drills.instructions: Two players stand 4-6 feet apart. The passer holds the ball with two hands, then uses a short underhand motion to shovel the ball to the receiver’s hands. The receiver catches with two hands and shovels it back. Keep the pass soft and short. Do 8 reps each side.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for short-pass touch, close-range passing, hand control, or low passing confidence. Assign if the player throws hard passes from too close or cannot control short passes. Use a lighter ball if the player cannot control the shovel motion.
drills.statistic: Not every pass needs power. Short touch passes help beginners learn feel, spacing, and control.
drills.safety: Do not shovel the ball at the face or stomach hard. Keep it soft.

drills.name: Wrap Pass Around Pad
drills.reps_target: slow, short, both sides
drills.instructions: A coach holds a soft pad or stands still as a safe obstacle. The passer stands a few feet away with a receiver on the other side. Make a controlled wrap pass around the pad to the receiver’s hands — around the obstacle, not over it. Start very slow and short.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low angle passing, poor ball protection, weak pass control, or turnover risk. Assign if the player throws straight into pressure or swings the ball out of control. Use no obstacle first if the player cannot pass accurately; younger players only if hand strength and control are safe.
drills.statistic: Passing around pressure is useful, but beginners need a safe obstacle and short distance first. This teaches angle without live defense.
drills.safety: Use a soft pad only. No live defender reaching or bumping.

drills.name: Dribble Pick-Up Pass
drills.reps_target: reps each hand
drills.instructions: Start with the ball and take two slow dribbles. Pick the ball up with two hands, stop the body, look at the target, and pass to a partner. The partner catches and passes back. Do reps with the right-hand dribble and the left-hand dribble.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor dribble-to-pass control, weak gather, low decision speed, or turnover risk. Assign if the player picks up the dribble and panics or throws without balance. Use one slow dribble first.
drills.statistic: Players need to connect ball handling and passing. This teaches a clean stop, gather, and pass without pressure.
drills.safety: No speed. Stop before passing.

drills.name: Jump Stop Pass
drills.reps_target: reps, short distance
drills.instructions: Start a few steps from a partner. Jog slowly forward, land in a soft jump stop, hold balance, and pass to the partner’s hands. The partner catches and returns the ball. Reset and repeat. Keep the distance short.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor stop control, weak passing balance, rushed passing, or travel risk. Assign if the player throws passes while falling forward or taking extra steps. Walk into the jump stop first if landing control is poor.
drills.statistic: A balanced stop makes the pass safer and more accurate. A low-speed way to combine footwork and passing.
drills.safety: Soft landing. No hard running starts.

drills.name: Pivot Find the Passer
drills.reps_target: reps, 2 targets then 3 if ready
drills.instructions: Start with the ball in the middle of the court. Two partners or coaches stand in different spots. Pivot slowly, find the coach who calls your name, and pass to that target. Get the ball back, reset, repeat. Start with two targets, add a third only if ready.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low court vision, panic passing, poor pivot control, or low decision-making. Assign if the player catches and throws without looking. Use one target first if the player gets overwhelmed.
drills.statistic: Passing decisions start with seeing the floor. This gives beginners a simple scan-and-pass habit.
drills.safety: Slow pivots only. Keep the ball protected.

drills.name: Receiver V-Cut Catch Pass
drills.reps_target: reps both sides
drills.instructions: A receiver starts a few steps from the passer. Walk or jog away at an angle, plant softly, cut back toward the ball, show hands, catch, and pass back. The passer gives a soft pass when the receiver comes back to the ball. Do both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low receiver movement, weak cutting timing, poor catch readiness, or low off-ball awareness. Assign if the player stands still waiting for passes or does not come back to the ball. Walk the V-cut first without the pass.
drills.statistic: Passing is easier when the receiver works to get open. V-cuts teach beginners that receiving is an active skill.
drills.safety: No sharp cuts at full speed. Keep it controlled.

drills.name: Stationary Give-Back Pass
drills.reps_target: 10 reps, then switch focus player
drills.instructions: Two players stand 6-8 feet apart. Player A passes to Player B. Player B catches, secures the ball for a half second, and passes it right back. The goal is quick but clean — do not slap the ball back without catching it. After 10 reps, switch focus player.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for slow ball movement, poor catch control, weak passing rhythm, or low confidence under simple tempo. Assign if the player holds the ball too long or rushes and bobbles the pass. Slow the pace if catches are not clean.
drills.statistic: Quick passing should still include a real catch. This teaches faster ball movement without skipping control.
drills.safety: Short distance. No hard passes.

drills.name: Three-Player Swing Pass
drills.reps_target: 30s, rest, repeat
drills.instructions: Three players stand in a line across the perimeter: wing, top, opposite wing. The ball starts on one wing. The first player passes to the top; the top passes to the opposite wing; then the ball comes back the same way. Show target hands and pass with control. Do 30 seconds, rest, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low swing passing, poor spacing, weak catch readiness, or low team rhythm. Assign if players hold the ball too long or do not understand moving the ball side to side. Move players closer for younger athletes.
drills.statistic: Swing passing teaches simple team ball movement — a safe beginner step before adding defenders or decisions.
drills.safety: Controlled passes only. No long skip passes for younger players.

drills.name: Four-Corner Short Pass
drills.reps_target: 30s, then reverse direction
drills.instructions: Set four cones in a small square; one player near each cone. The ball moves around the square with short controlled passes. Each player catches, calls the next player’s name, and passes. After 30 seconds, reverse direction. Keep the square small for younger players.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low group passing, poor communication, weak catch readiness, or low spacing awareness. Assign if players crowd each other or pass without calling names. Use three players in a triangle if numbers are limited.
drills.statistic: Small-shape passing teaches spacing and target passing without needing speed or defense, and keeps younger players organized.
drills.safety: Keep passes short. Make sure each player is watching.

drills.name: Inbound Target Pass
drills.reps_target: reps from baseline and sideline
drills.instructions: Stand out of bounds with the ball; a receiver stands a short distance inbounds showing target hands. Say the receiver’s name, step safely behind the line, and pass to the target. The receiver catches and gives the ball back. Do reps from the baseline and sideline.
