drills.coaching_notes: Best for low inbound confidence, poor target passing, weak communication, or turnover risk. Assign if the player panics when inbounding or throws the ball into traffic. Keep receiver very close for younger players.
drills.statistic: Inbounding is a common turnover spot for beginners. This makes the pass simple, calm, and target-based.
drills.safety: No defenders at first. Keep the pass short and safe.

drills.name: Sideline Advance Pass
drills.reps_target: reps, shorten distance for young players
drills.instructions: A passer starts near the backcourt sideline with the ball. A receiver starts 10-15 feet ahead on the same sideline and shows hands. The passer makes a controlled pass up the sideline. The receiver catches, secures, and passes back or to the coach. Shorten the distance for younger players.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low advance-pass awareness, poor sideline accuracy, weak passing strength, or over-dribbling habit. Assign if the player dribbles into trouble instead of making an easy pass ahead. Use stationary short passes first if distance is too hard; ages 7-8 only with very short distance.
drills.statistic: Passing ahead can beat pressure and save dribbles. Beginners need short, safe advance passes before long transition passing.
drills.safety: No long heaves. Keep distance strength-appropriate.

drills.name: Weak-Hand Push Pass Close
drills.reps_target: 6-8 reps, then rest
drills.instructions: Stand 4-6 feet from a partner. Hold the ball with two hands, then use the weak hand to push the ball softly to the partner’s hands. The partner catches and passes back. Do 6-8 reps, then rest. Keep the pass short and controlled.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for weak-hand control, low passing variety, poor hand strength, or one-sided passing. Assign if the player cannot pass with the weak hand at all or always turns into pressure. Use two-hand passes first if the weak hand cannot control the ball; ages 7-8 only with a smaller ball and very short distance.
drills.statistic: Weak-hand passing gives players more options, but young players need short distance and the right ball size first.
drills.safety: Short distance only. No whipping the ball.

drills.name: Pass Around the Circle
drills.reps_target: 1 min, then reverse direction
drills.instructions: Players stand in a circle. The ball moves around the circle in order. Each player catches, pivots slightly toward the next player, calls their name, and passes. After one minute, reverse direction. For younger groups, keep the circle small and use soft passes.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low group awareness, poor catching, weak communication, or low passing rhythm. Assign if players are not ready when the ball comes around or pass without looking. Use fewer players or a smaller circle if attention is low.
drills.statistic: Group passing helps young players learn timing and readiness. It is simple, organized, and low pressure.
drills.safety: No surprise passes. Make sure the next player is looking.

drills.name: Coach Point Passing Choice
drills.reps_target: slow, add 3rd receiver if ready
drills.instructions: Two receivers stand in different spots; the passer starts with the ball. The coach points to one receiver. The passer looks, steps, and passes to that receiver. The receiver catches and passes back to the coach or passer. Start slow. Add a third receiver only if ready.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low decision-making, poor visual scanning, weak passing accuracy, or panic passing. Assign if the player passes without reading or gets overwhelmed by multiple targets. Use one receiver first if the player struggles.
drills.statistic: Decision drills do not need to be complex for beginners. A coach point gives a simple visual cue and teaches the player to look before passing.
drills.safety: No yelling or rushing. Keep passes controlled.

drills.name: Safe Pass Under Light Shadow
drills.reps_target: reps, short passes, no movement first
drills.instructions: A passer stands with the ball. A coach or defender stands a step away with hands out but does not steal or touch the ball. The passer pivots, protects the ball, and passes to a receiver’s hands. Start with short passes and no movement. The defender is only a shadow.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low pressure confidence, poor ball protection, weak pivot passing, or panic under a defender. Assign if the player is safe with no pressure but panics when someone stands nearby. Remove the shadow if the player turns away, freezes, or throws wildly; younger players only if calm and safe.
drills.statistic: Pressure should be layered slowly. A shadow defender teaches calm passing without steals, contact, or chaos.
drills.safety: No reaching, no trapping, no contact. Shadow only.

drills.name: Pass Accuracy Ladder
drills.reps_target: 5 accurate passes per mark, move back if clean
drills.instructions: Place three floor marks at short, medium, and slightly longer beginner distances. Start at the closest mark and make 5 accurate passes to a partner’s hands. If clean and safe, move back one mark. If passes get weak, wild, or unsafe, move back in. Use the player’s real strength level, not their age ego.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low passing strength, poor distance control, weak accuracy, or forced long passes. Assign if the player tries to throw passes farther than they can safely control. Use only the closest mark for younger or low-strength players.
drills.statistic: Passing range should match strength. This finds the player’s clean passing distance and protects mechanics.
drills.safety: Do not move back if the pass gets unsafe. Clean short passes beat wild long passes.

drills.name: Fingertip Balance Hold
drills.reps_target: 8-10 reps
drills.instructions: Stand still with the ball in both hands. Hold the ball lightly on the fingertips at chest height for 3 seconds, then pull it into the chest with strong hands. Reset and repeat. Do 8-10 reps. Younger players use a smaller or lighter ball so the hold does not turn into a strain.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low hand strength, poor ball feel, weak catch security, or low ball comfort. Assign if the player palms the ball awkwardly, drops simple catches, or cannot hold the ball with control. Use a smaller ball if the player cannot hold it without pain or strain.
drills.statistic: Younger players often lack the hand strength to control a full-size ball. This builds fingertip awareness before harder passing or ball handling.
drills.safety: No squeezing through pain. Use the right ball size.

drills.name: Ball Flip and Secure
drills.reps_target: 8 clean catches, rest, repeat
drills.instructions: Hold the ball with two hands at waist height. Flip it lightly upward, let it rotate once if possible, catch with two hands, and pull it into the chest. Keep the flip low and controlled. Do 8 clean catches, rest, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor ball tracking, weak soft hands, low catch control, or low hand-eye coordination. Assign if the player struggles to secure the ball after it moves or rotates. Use a foam or smaller ball if the player is afraid of catching.
drills.statistic: Playmaking starts with ball control. A player who cannot secure a small self-flip will struggle with faster passes from teammates.
drills.safety: Keep the flip below the face. No high tosses.

drills.name: Low Pocket Carry Walk
drills.reps_target: 2-3 trips
drills.instructions: Hold the ball tight near one hip or low pocket area with two hands. Walk 10 steps forward, stop, switch the ball to the other side, and walk back. Keep the ball close, eyes forward, and body calm. Do 2-3 trips.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor ball security, low body control, weak grip, or high turnover risk. Assign if the player carries the ball loose, swings it away from the body, or loses it when moving. Use a smaller ball if the player cannot hold it close safely.
drills.statistic: Some beginners need to learn how to simply own the ball before they can pass or dribble well. Ball security is a base playmaking skill.
drills.safety: Walk only. No running or contact.

drills.name: Protect the Ball Turn
drills.reps_target: 5 turns each direction
drills.instructions: Stand still with the ball held strong near the chest or side pocket. On the coach cue, turn the body 90 degrees while keeping the ball tight, then turn back. Do 5 turns each direction. Move slowly and stay balanced.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor ball protection, weak body control, low pivot awareness, or turnover risk. Assign if the player turns with the ball away from the body or loses control under light pressure. Use no pivot-foot emphasis at first if footwork is confusing.
drills.statistic: A lot of turnovers happen because players turn into pressure with the ball exposed. This teaches a safer body-and-ball relationship.
drills.safety: No spinning fast. Keep the turn slow and balanced.

drills.name: Eyes-Up Dribble Scan
drills.reps_target: 10s, rest, repeat
drills.instructions: Dribble in place or walk slowly with the ball. A coach stands in front and holds up fingers, colors, or simple signs. Call out what you see while keeping the dribble alive. Start with 10 seconds, rest, repeat. Younger players use a lower bounce and the strong hand first.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low eyes-up control, poor dribble awareness, weak court vision, or low playmaking confidence. Assign if the player cannot dribble and see a teammate or coach at the same time. Use stationary ball control first if the player cannot dribble safely; ages 7-8 use a smaller ball and very short reps.
drills.statistic: A playmaker has to see the floor. This keeps the ball task simple while adding a safe visual cue.
drills.safety: No speed. Keep space clear.

drills.name: Red Light Green Light Dribble Control
drills.reps_target: short space, control not racing
drills.instructions: Players line up with a ball. On "green," dribble forward slowly. On "red," stop the body and keep control of the ball. On "yellow," slow down but keep dribbling. Start in a short space. The goal is control, not racing.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor start-stop control, low dribble control, weak listening response, or high lost-ball rate. Assign if the player runs faster than they can control the ball. Use walking speed and smaller balls for younger athletes.
drills.statistic: Young athletes need start-stop control before faster ball handling. This keeps playmaking fun while teaching control.
drills.safety: No racing. Keep players spaced apart.

drills.name: Color Cone Dribble Choice
drills.reps_target: reps, strong hand first
drills.instructions: Place three colored cones in front of the player. Start with the ball. The coach calls a color. Dribble slowly to that cone, stop under control, protect the ball, and reset. Start with the strong hand. Add weak hand only if control is safe.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low decision speed, poor dribble control, weak stop control, or low court awareness. Assign if the player loses the ball when asked to think while dribbling. Use two cones only for younger players.
drills.statistic: Decision-making should start small. A color call gives the player a simple playmaking read without adding pressure.
drills.safety: No sprinting. Stop before turning.

drills.name: Partner Mirror Dribble Control
drills.reps_target: 10-15s, rest, switch leaders
drills.instructions: Two players face each other, each with a ball. Player A leads, dribbling in place while changing body height, hand, or slow side steps. Player B mirrors while keeping control. Go 10-15 seconds, rest, switch leaders. Keep it slow for beginners.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low reaction control, poor eyes-up dribbling, weak coordination, or low focus. Assign if the player can dribble alone but loses control when watching another person. Use one leader with no ball for younger players; ages 7-8 only with very simple stationary versions.
drills.statistic: Playmaking requires reacting to other players. This adds a teammate cue while keeping the movement low-pressure.
drills.safety: Keep space between players. No fast lateral moves.

drills.name: Dribble Circle Keep-In
drills.reps_target: 10-15s, strong hand first
drills.instructions: Create a small circle with cones or use a painted circle on the court. Dribble inside the circle for 10-15 seconds without stepping out or losing the ball — walk or shuffle slowly. Start with the strong hand. Add weak hand later if safe.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor space control, low dribble control, weak body awareness, or high lost-ball rate. Assign if the player needs too much space to control the dribble. Make the circle bigger for younger players.
drills.statistic: Players need to control the ball in limited space before handling pressure. This teaches safe space awareness without defenders.
drills.safety: No crowding. One player per circle.

drills.name: Dribble Stop Show Target
drills.reps_target: reps, short distance
drills.instructions: Take three slow dribbles forward. On the coach cue, stop, pick the ball up with two hands, secure it, then show target hands to the coach. The coach gives a soft return pass, and the player catches. Reset and repeat. Keep the distance short.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor dribble stop control, weak catch readiness, low ball security, or low playmaking awareness. Assign if the player stops the dribble and does not know what to do next. Use one dribble only if control is poor.
drills.statistic: A player who stops dribbling becomes a passer or receiver again. This teaches the transition from ball handler to ready teammate.
drills.safety: No fast stops. Secure the ball before showing hands.

drills.name: Receiver Backpedal Catch
drills.reps_target: 6-8 reps, then switch roles
drills.instructions: A receiver starts 4-6 feet from the passer. Take two slow backpedal steps, show hands, and catch a soft pass. After the catch, stop, secure the ball, and pass it back. Start slow and keep the pass soft. Do 6-8 reps, switch roles.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor moving catch, weak balance, low receiver control, or low spacing awareness. Assign if the player cannot catch while moving away from the passer. Use stationary catching first if balance is poor; ages 7-8 only with walking steps and very soft passes.
drills.statistic: Receivers do not always move toward the ball. Sometimes they create space by moving out or back. This teaches that safely.
drills.safety: Check space behind the receiver. No fast backpedaling.

drills.name: Receiver Slide Catch
drills.reps_target: reps both directions
drills.instructions: A receiver starts in front of a passer. On the coach cue, slide two steps to the side, show hands, and catch a soft pass. Secure the ball and pass back. Do both directions. Keep the slide slow and the pass short.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low lateral control, poor catch balance, weak receiver movement, or low spacing skill. Assign if the player only catches standing still and struggles moving to open space. Walk sideways instead of sliding for younger players.
drills.statistic: Playmakers need receivers who move into passing windows. This teaches simple side movement and catch control.
drills.safety: No fast slides. Keep feet under control.

drills.name: Give-and-Follow Pass
drills.reps_target: 30s, slow
drills.instructions: Three players stand in a short line or triangle. Player A passes to Player B, then follows the pass to Player B’s spot. Player B passes to Player C and follows. Player C passes to Player A’s new spot and follows. Keep passes short and controlled. Go slowly for 30 seconds.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low pass-and-move habit, poor spacing, weak passing rhythm, or low team awareness. Assign if the player passes and stays frozen. Walk the pattern first without the ball.
drills.statistic: Passing should create movement. Give-and-follow teaches a simple team habit without adding defenders or speed.
drills.safety: Walk first. No running into the receiver.

drills.name: Triangle Catch-Turn-Pass
drills.reps_target: 30s, then reverse direction
drills.instructions: Three players form a small triangle. Player A passes to Player B. Player B catches, turns the body toward Player C, and passes. Player C catches, turns, and passes to Player A. Keep the ball moving slowly. Reverse direction after 30 seconds.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor body control, low passing rhythm, weak catch security, or low group awareness. Assign if the player catches and passes without turning to the next target. Use a smaller triangle for younger players.
drills.statistic: A player often has to catch facing one direction and pass another. This teaches that body turn in a safe, organized way.
drills.safety: No hard passes. Make sure each player is watching.

drills.name: Dribble Draw Two Pass
drills.reps_target: reps, no live defender
drills.instructions: Place a cone or coach near the lane as the help defender. A ball handler starts on the wing with a teammate in the corner or short wing. Dribble slowly toward the cone, stop before the cone, and pass to the teammate. The teammate catches and secures the ball. Start with no live defender.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low drive-and-kick awareness, poor decision timing, weak passing under movement, or high turnover risk. Assign if the player dribbles into help and does not pass to the open teammate. Use stationary coach point passing first if the decision is too hard; ages 8-9 only with very slow speed and short pass distance.
drills.statistic: Playmaking means knowing when the defense has helped. This gives the player a clear, safe cue to pass before pressure gets real.
drills.safety: No live defense. Stop before the cone. No collisions.

drills.name: Look-Off Target Pass
drills.reps_target: reps, switch sides, short passes
drills.instructions: Two receivers stand close, one on each side. The passer looks briefly at Receiver A, then passes to Receiver B’s target hands. Then switch sides. The look-off should be small and controlled. The passer must still step and pass with balance. Start with very short passes.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low vision control, predictable passing, poor target accuracy, or low decision confidence. Assign if the player telegraphs every pass but can already make safe short passes. Use coach point passing first if the player cannot handle two targets; younger players only if basic passing is already safe.
drills.statistic: Deception should be small for beginners. This teaches eye control without wild fakes or risky passes.
drills.safety: No hard passes. Do not use if the player is still missing basic targets.

drills.name: Trap Calm Pivot Pass
drills.reps_target: very short reps
drills.instructions: Start with the ball. Two coaches or teammates stand nearby as soft shadows with hands up, but they do not reach or touch. Keep the ball protected, pivot slowly, find the open receiver, and pass. The receiver catches and returns the ball. Start with very short reps.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low trap confidence, poor pivot passing, weak ball protection, or panic passing. Assign if the player freezes or throws wildly when two defenders are nearby. Use one shadow defender first if the player panics; younger players only if calm and safe.
drills.statistic: Pressure should be introduced in layers. This gives the player a trap picture without steals, contact, or chaos.
drills.safety: No reaching, no trapping contact, no yelling. Shadows only.

drills.name: Middle Flash Catch and Pass
drills.reps_target: reps both sides
drills.instructions: Start on the wing or short corner. Flash to the middle area, show hands, catch a soft pass, turn under control, and pass to another teammate or coach. Do not rush after the catch. Do reps from both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low middle-catch confidence, poor receiver movement, weak pass-after-catch skill, or low team awareness. Assign if the player catches in the middle and panics or forces a shot. Use a stationary middle catch first if movement is hard.
drills.statistic: Some of the best beginner playmaking is simple catch-and-move-the-ball work. This teaches the player to connect the offense.
drills.safety: No defenders at first. Keep the middle area clear.

drills.name: Two-Spot Decision Pass
drills.reps_target: reps, switch ready receiver
drills.instructions: Two receivers stand at short, safe distances. The passer starts with the ball in the middle. One receiver shows hands while the other keeps hands down. The passer must pass only to the receiver showing hands. Switch which receiver is ready each rep. Keep the pass short and easy.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor decision-making, low visual awareness, weak target recognition, or panic passing. Assign if the player passes to teammates who are not ready or throws without looking. Use one target first if two choices are too much.
drills.statistic: Beginners need simple decisions before live defense. Target hands give the passer a clear cue for who is ready.
drills.safety: No fake surprise passes. Keep all players watching.

drills.name: Ball Control Relay Walk
drills.reps_target: relay, walking only
drills.instructions: Players line up in small teams. The first player walks to a cone holding the ball securely, walks around the cone, comes back, and hands the ball to the next player. The next player repeats. Start with walking only. The goal is clean control and a safe handoff, not speed.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low ball security, poor movement control, weak handoff control, or low team confidence. Assign if the player drops the ball while moving or struggles handing it to a teammate. Use a smaller ball or shorter walking distance.
drills.statistic: For very young players, playmaking starts with safe control and sharing the ball. This low-load relay builds comfort before harder passing games.
drills.safety: Walking only. No racing or pushing.

drills.name: Floor Tap Ball Control
drills.reps_target: 8-10 slow reps, rest, repeat
drills.instructions: Stand with the ball in both hands. Bend the knees, tap the ball lightly to the floor with two hands, then bring it back to the chest. Keep the back flat, eyes forward when possible, ball under control. Do 8-10 slow reps, rest, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low ball familiarity, weak grip, poor body control, or low hand confidence. Assign if the player drops the ball when bending, cannot control it near the floor, or looks uncomfortable holding it. Use a smaller or lighter ball if the player cannot control it safely.
drills.statistic: Very young players often need low-load ball control before passing. This builds comfort with the ball while keeping speed, pressure, and impact low.
drills.safety: Bend the knees, not just the back. No fast slams.

drills.name: Knee Tap Ball Switch
drills.reps_target: 6 taps each side
drills.instructions: Stand with feet shoulder-width and the ball in both hands. Tap the ball lightly to the outside of the right knee, bring it back to the middle, then tap it to the outside of the left knee. Stay slow and balanced. Do 6 taps each side.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor coordination, low ball control, weak body awareness, or low grip comfort. Assign if the player loses the ball when moving it across the body. Use a smaller ball if the player cannot move it cleanly side to side.
drills.statistic: Side-to-side control helps players learn where the ball is without staring down the whole time — a safe low-rung ball-control drill.
drills.safety: Keep the movement slow. Do not twist the knees.

drills.name: Ball Hug and Release
drills.reps_target: reps, add soft toss only if ready
drills.instructions: Start with the ball. Hug the ball to the chest for 2 seconds, then extend it forward with two hands like ready to pass. Bring it back in, reset, and repeat. Add a soft partner toss only if the player is ready.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low ball security, weak catch confidence, poor hand strength, or fear of the ball. Assign if the player catches and drops the ball, holds it away from the body, or freezes after catching. Use a foam ball if the player is scared of the ball.
drills.statistic: Some athletes need to learn safe ownership of the ball before making passes. Securing the ball is the first step in playmaking.
drills.safety: No squeezing through pain. Keep shoulders relaxed.

drills.name: Partner Hand-Off Exchange
drills.reps_target: 8-10 clean exchanges
drills.instructions: Two players stand close together. Player A holds the ball with two hands and says the teammate’s name. Player B shows both hands. Player A places the ball into Player B’s hands. Player B secures it, says "got it," then hands it back. Do 8-10 clean exchanges.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low hand readiness, poor ball sharing, weak catch security, or low communication. Assign if the player is not ready for thrown passes yet. Use a smaller ball if the exchange feels awkward.
drills.statistic: A hand-off is a lower rung than a pass. It lets younger players learn receiver hands, communication, and ball security without fear.
drills.safety: No pulling or grabbing the ball away. Clean hand-to-hand exchange only.

drills.name: Name and Hand-Off Circle
drills.reps_target: slow, small circle
drills.instructions: Players stand in a small circle. One player holds the ball, says a teammate’s name, walks the ball to that teammate, and hands it to them. The receiver says "got it," secures the ball, then chooses the next teammate. Keep the circle small and slow.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low teammate awareness, weak communication, poor ball security, or low confidence. Assign if players do not call names, do not show hands, or are not ready to receive. Use fewer players if attention span is low.
drills.statistic: Communication is part of playmaking. For very young players, walking a hand-off can be more age-appropriate than thrown passes.
drills.safety: Walking only. No racing or throwing.

drills.name: Dribble to Hug Stop
drills.reps_target: 6-8 reps, strong hand first
drills.instructions: Take 3 slow dribbles forward. On the coach cue, pick up the ball with two hands and hug it to the chest. Hold for 2 seconds, then reset. Do 6-8 reps. Start with the strong hand, then use the weak hand only if safe.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor dribble stop control, weak ball security, low hand strength, or high turnover risk. Assign if the player stops the dribble and fumbles the ball. Use one dribble first if the player cannot pick the ball up cleanly.
drills.statistic: A player has to secure the ball before making the next play. This is a low-pressure bridge from dribbling to passing.
drills.safety: No fast stops. Keep eyes up when possible.

drills.name: Dribble to Coach Name Pass
drills.reps_target: reps, short passes, no pressure
drills.instructions: Two coaches or teammates stand in front at short distance. Dribble slowly in place or forward. One coach calls your name. Stop, secure the ball, look at that coach, and pass softly to their hands. Start with short passes and no pressure.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low dribble-to-pass control, poor listening response, weak decision-making, or low court awareness. Assign if the player dribbles with head down and cannot react to a teammate call. Use one receiver first if the player gets overwhelmed; ages 7-8 only with very short distance and simple cues.
drills.statistic: Playmaking starts with hearing and seeing teammates. This adds one simple decision after the dribble but keeps pressure out.
drills.safety: No fast dribbling. Stop before passing.

drills.name: Pass to Moving Hands
drills.reps_target: reps, keep it slow
drills.instructions: A receiver stands 6-8 feet away and slowly moves their target hands from chest level to outside shoulder level. The passer waits until the target is clear, then passes softly to the hands. The receiver catches, resets the hands, and passes back. Keep it slow.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low target tracking, poor pass placement, weak teammate awareness, or rushed passing. Assign if the player throws before the receiver is ready or misses changing targets. Use still target hands first if accuracy is poor.
drills.statistic: Receivers are not statues. This teaches the passer to see the target before throwing.
drills.safety: No face-level targets. Keep passes soft.

drills.name: Receiver Call for Ball
drills.reps_target: reps both sides
drills.instructions: A passer stands with the ball; the receiver starts a few steps away. The receiver must say "ball" or call the passer’s name while showing hands. Only then can the passer pass. The receiver catches, secures the ball, and passes back. Do reps from both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low communication, poor receiver readiness, weak catch confidence, or low teammate awareness. Assign if the player waits silently or hides hands when they are open. Let shy players start with a quieter call and build up.
drills.statistic: Playmaking is not only the passer’s job. Receivers help create good passes by communicating and showing a target.
drills.safety: No surprise passes. Receiver must be ready first.

drills.name: Two-Hand Push to Floor Spot
drills.reps_target: 8-10 reps
drills.instructions: Place a floor spot, hoop, or flat marker 5-8 feet away. Start with the ball at the chest and push it with two hands so it lands or rolls toward the target. Retrieve the ball and repeat. The pass should be controlled, not slammed. Do 8-10 reps.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low passing strength, poor aim, weak shoulder control, or low confidence. Assign if the player cannot safely throw a pass to a partner yet. Use roll pass drills first if pushing still feels too hard.
drills.statistic: Younger players often need a target task before live partner passing. This keeps force low and builds aim.
drills.safety: No hard slams. Keep the target flat and safe.

drills.name: Soft Bounce to Partner Hands
drills.reps_target: 8-10 reps
drills.instructions: Two players stand close. The passer makes a soft bounce pass to the receiver’s hands. The receiver catches, secures the ball, and gives a soft bounce pass back. Remind the passer the ball should come up to the hands, not stay at the feet. Do 8-10 reps.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low bounce touch, poor pass height, weak catch timing, or low passing accuracy. Assign if bounce passes die at the feet or pop up too high. Shorten distance or use a smaller ball for younger players.
drills.statistic: Bounce passing is about touch and placement. This keeps it short and safe while teaching the ball to rise to the receiver.
drills.safety: No hard bounce passes. Keep distance short.

drills.name: Pass Through Low Window
drills.reps_target: 8 clean passes, then switch roles
drills.instructions: Place two cones or flat markers a few feet apart on the floor. The passer stands close and passes the ball through the low window to a partner — a soft bounce or low push pass depending on strength. After 8 clean passes, switch roles.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low accuracy, poor passing lane awareness, weak touch, or high turnover risk. Assign if the player passes into crowded space or cannot aim between simple markers. Make the window wider for younger players.
drills.statistic: A low window gives the player a clear passing lane. It builds direction and touch before adding defenders.
drills.safety: Use flat markers if possible. No raised obstacles that cause trips.

drills.name: Pass Through High Window
drills.reps_target: reps, short distance only
drills.instructions: A coach holds a pool noodle or foam stick low and away from the players. The passer stands close and passes over the noodle to a receiver’s hands — soft and controlled. Use short distance only. Switch roles after a few reps.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low arc control, poor pass touch, weak overhead awareness, or limited passing variety. Assign if the player throws every air pass too high, too hard, or too flat. Use low-window passing first if control is poor; ages 8-9 only with a very soft ball and short distance.
drills.statistic: Some passes need to clear hands or bodies, but beginners should learn that with a safe obstacle and short distance first.
drills.safety: Use soft obstacles only. No hard contests or high-speed throws.

drills.name: One Dribble Side-Step Pass
drills.reps_target: reps both directions
drills.instructions: Start with the ball and a partner in front; place a cone between them as an imaginary defender. Take one slow dribble to the side, stop, and pass around the cone to the partner’s hands. Repeat both directions. Keep the pass short and controlled.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor passing angles, low dribble-to-pass control, weak decision-making, or high turnover risk. Assign if the player throws into a blocked lane instead of moving to create a clear pass. Use no-dribble side-step first if the dribble is not controlled; younger players only with very slow speed and short distance.
drills.statistic: Playmakers do not always need a hard move. Sometimes one controlled dribble creates a safe passing lane.
drills.safety: No speed. Stop before passing.

drills.name: No-Dribble Side-Step Pass
drills.reps_target: reps both sides, start close
drills.instructions: Stand with the ball. A cone sits between passer and receiver as an imaginary defender. Step to the side with balance, keep the ball protected, and pass around the cone to the receiver’s hands. Reset and repeat both sides. Start close.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor passing angles, weak footwork, low ball protection, or high turnover risk. Assign if the player throws straight into pressure or does not know how to move before passing. Move the cone farther away if the lane is too tight.
drills.statistic: A simple side step can open a safe pass — lower load than dribble movement and better for younger players not ready to handle and pass at the same time.
drills.safety: Step short. No lunging or twisting.

drills.name: Receiver Seal Hands Catch
drills.reps_target: 8-10 clean catches
drills.instructions: A receiver stands close to a passer and shows both hands. The passer gives a soft pass. The receiver catches, closes both hands around the ball, and pulls it into the chest, then passes it back. Do 8-10 clean catches. Coach cues "catch, seal, secure."
drills.coaching_notes: Best for weak catch security, low hand strength, poor soft hands, or fumbled passes. Assign if passes hit the hands but pop out. Use a smaller or softer ball if the player cannot catch safely.
drills.statistic: Some players touch the ball but do not secure it. Catching is not complete until the player seals the ball.
drills.safety: Soft passes. No passes above shoulder height for younger players.

drills.name: Coach Call Protect or Pass
drills.reps_target: 8-10 reps, slow calls
drills.instructions: Start with the ball. A coach stands nearby and calls either "protect" or "pass." On "protect," bring the ball tight to the body and turn slightly away. On "pass," pass softly to a nearby receiver. Do 8-10 reps with slow calls.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low listening response, poor ball security, weak decision-making, or panic passing. Assign if the player passes when they should secure the ball or freezes when told to pass. Use only one call at first if the player gets confused.
drills.statistic: Decision-making starts with simple choices. This gives the player two safe options before pressure is added.
drills.safety: No pressure or yelling. Keep the choices calm.

drills.name: Strong-Side Weak-Side Point
drills.reps_target: reps, then add a soft pass
drills.instructions: A coach stands with the ball on one side of the court; the player stands in the middle. The coach asks "strong side?" and the player points to the ball side. Then "weak side?" and the player points away from the ball. After a few correct reps, the player catches a soft pass and points again.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low court awareness, poor spacing understanding, weak team-concept knowledge, or low playmaking IQ. Assign if the player does not know where the ball side or help side is. Use "ball side" and "away side" language for younger players.
drills.statistic: Playmaking is easier when the player understands where the ball is and where space is. A simple first step toward better decisions.
drills.safety: No movement pressure. Teach first.

drills.name: Receiver Window Step
drills.reps_target: reps both sides
drills.instructions: Place two cones as an imaginary defender lane between passer and receiver. The receiver starts behind the lane, then takes one step to the side into open space and shows hands. The passer throws a soft pass. The receiver catches, secures, and passes back. Work both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low receiver spacing, poor passing-lane awareness, weak catch readiness, or low off-ball awareness. Assign if the receiver stands behind defenders or does not move into a passing window. Make the window wider and use walking speed for younger players.
drills.statistic: The receiver has a job too. A small step into a passing window makes the pass safer and teaches spacing.
drills.safety: No hard cuts. Step, show hands, catch.

drills.name: Two-Touch Control Pass
drills.reps_target: 10 controlled reps
drills.instructions: Two players stand close. Player A passes softly to Player B. Player B catches, taps it once to the chest to secure it, then passes back — two touches: catch, secure, pass. Do not volley the ball back. Do 10 controlled reps, then change rhythm or distance only if safe.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor catch control, rushed passing, weak rhythm, or fumbled ball movement. Assign if the player rushes passes back without really catching first. Use a smaller ball or shorter distance if catches are not clean.
drills.statistic: Quick passing still needs control. This teaches rhythm without letting the player skip the catch.
drills.safety: Soft passes only. Control before speed.

drills.name: Ball Carry Change Hands
drills.reps_target: 8-10 slow transfers
drills.instructions: Stand still with the ball held tight on the right side of the body. Move the ball across the chest to the left side, hold for 2 seconds, then move it back to the right. Keep the ball close to the body. Do 8-10 slow transfers. Younger players use a smaller ball.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low hand strength, poor ball control, weak transfer control, or low ball security. Assign if the player drops the ball when moving it across the body. Use a smaller ball or fewer reps if the player strains to hold it.
drills.statistic: Young players often lose the ball because it is too big, too heavy, or poorly controlled. This builds safe control before passing speed is added.
drills.safety: No swinging the ball fast. Keep it close to the chest.

drills.name: Ball Around One Leg
drills.reps_target: 5 circles each leg
drills.instructions: Stand with one foot slightly forward. Move the ball around the front leg in a small circle, passing it from hand to hand. Do 5 circles around the right leg, then 5 around the left. Start slow; do not bend too far or lose balance.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor coordination, weak hand transfer, low ball comfort, or poor body control. Assign if the player struggles moving the ball around the legs without dropping it. Use around-the-waist control drills first if this is too hard.
drills.statistic: Body ball-control drills help young players learn where the ball is without relying only on dribbling, supporting better control when passing and catching later.
drills.safety: Keep the bend small. Stop if the player loses balance.

drills.name: Ball Tap Walk
drills.reps_target: 10 steps out and back
drills.instructions: Tap the ball lightly between both hands at chest height while walking 10 steps forward. Turn around and walk back keeping the taps controlled. The ball should not go near the face. Start slow and use a smaller ball if needed.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor hand control, low movement coordination, weak ball familiarity, or low confidence. Assign if the player can tap the ball standing still but loses it while walking. Stand still first if walking causes drops.
drills.statistic: Playmaking happens while moving. This gives young players a low-pressure way to carry ball control into movement.
drills.safety: Walk only. Keep eyes forward when possible.

drills.name: Pocket Protect Walk
drills.reps_target: 2-3 trips
drills.instructions: Hold the ball tight near the outside hip with two hands. Walk from one cone to another, keeping the ball close and protected. At the cone, switch the ball to the other hip and walk back. Do 2-3 trips.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor ball protection, weak grip, high turnover risk, or low body control. Assign if the player carries the ball loose or exposes it while moving. Use shorter walking distance for younger players.
drills.statistic: Ball security is part of playmaking. A player who cannot protect the ball while moving will struggle before they ever make the pass.
drills.safety: Walking only. No contact or defenders.

drills.name: Partner Chest Target Catch Only
drills.reps_target: 8 clean catches
drills.instructions: A coach or partner stands close and gives a soft pass to the player’s chest target. Show hands, catch with two hands, pull the ball in, and hold it for 2 seconds. The coach takes the ball back and repeats. Do 8 clean catches.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low catch confidence, poor hand readiness, weak ball security, or fear of the ball. Assign if the player cannot catch safely enough to return passes. Use a foam ball first if the player flinches.
drills.statistic: Some players are not ready for full partner passing. Removing the return pass lets them focus on catching first.
drills.safety: Soft passes only. No face-level throws.

drills.name: Receiver Step-In Catch
drills.reps_target: 8 reps, then switch roles
drills.instructions: A receiver starts one step behind a floor marker; a passer stands close. As the passer starts the pass, the receiver steps to the marker, shows hands, catches, and secures the ball. The receiver passes back softly or hands the ball back. Do 8 reps, switch roles.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor receiver timing, low catch strength, weak ball security, or low pass awareness. Assign if the player waits for the ball instead of moving into the catch. Walk through the step without a pass first.
drills.statistic: A good receiver helps the passer. Stepping into the catch reduces lazy turnovers and builds stronger hands.
drills.safety: One short step only. No lunging.

drills.name: Pass to Coach’s Pocket
drills.reps_target: reps, change target every few
drills.instructions: A coach stands 6-8 feet away and shows a target near the right pocket, left pocket, or chest. Throw a soft controlled pass to that exact target. The coach changes the target every few reps. Step, aim, and pass with control.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low pass placement, poor target accuracy, weak teammate awareness, or high turnover risk. Assign if the player throws passes to random spots instead of the receiver’s target. Use one target only if the player struggles.
drills.statistic: Good playmakers place the ball where the receiver can use it. This starts with clear pocket targets at short range.
drills.safety: Do not target the face. Keep passes soft and close.

drills.name: Soft Pass Over Line
drills.reps_target: 8-10 reps
drills.instructions: Place a flat line or tape mark between passer and receiver. The passer must send the ball softly over the line to the receiver’s hands — not hard or wild. The receiver catches, secures, and passes back. Do 8-10 reps.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor pass touch, low distance control, weak accuracy, or hard passes. Assign if the player throws every pass too hard or cannot control distance. Shorten the distance for younger players.
drills.statistic: Pass touch matters as much as strength. This gives the player a small target task without making the pass long.
drills.safety: Use flat tape only. No raised obstacle.

drills.name: Pass to Stationary Hoop Target
drills.reps_target: 8-10 reps
drills.instructions: Place a hula hoop, flat circle, or marked target on the floor. Stand 5-8 feet away and pass the ball so it lands in or near the target — a soft bounce, push, or roll depending on strength. Do 8-10 reps.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low aim, weak passing accuracy, low confidence, or poor force control. Assign if the player misses a partner badly or cannot control pass direction. Move closer or use a bigger target for younger players.
drills.statistic: Some athletes need target practice before partner passing. It removes fear of hitting a teammate and lets the player work on direction.
drills.safety: Keep rolling balls away from other players’ feet.

drills.name: Short Pass After Catch Turn
drills.reps_target: reps both turn directions
drills.instructions: Start facing a passer. The passer gives a soft pass. Catch, turn the shoulders toward a second target, and pass softly — do not rush the turn. Use short distances and no defenders. Do both turn directions.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low catch-turn control, poor body alignment, weak pass accuracy, or rushed passing. Assign if the player catches and passes without facing the target. Practice catch-turn without passing first.
drills.statistic: Players often catch from one angle and pass to another. This builds the turn before the pass.
drills.safety: Turn slowly. No twisting hard through the knees.

drills.name: Receiver Circle Step Catch
drills.reps_target: 5 catches each direction
drills.instructions: Place a cone on the floor. The receiver walks around the cone in a small circle. The passer gives a soft pass when the receiver comes back toward the ball. The receiver catches, secures, and passes back. Do 5 catches clockwise and 5 counterclockwise.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor moving catch, low receiver control, weak balance, or low timing. Assign if the player can catch standing still but struggles when moving. Walk slower or make the circle smaller.
drills.statistic: Moving catches should start with walking patterns. This gives the receiver movement without speed or pressure.
drills.safety: Walk only. Keep the cone away from the feet.

drills.name: Dribble Pause Look Pass
drills.reps_target: reps, strong hand first
drills.instructions: Dribble slowly in place or forward. On the coach cue, pause the body while keeping control of the ball, look up at a receiver, pick the ball up, and pass softly. The receiver catches and returns the ball. Start with strong-hand dribble only.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low court vision, poor dribble-to-pass timing, weak decision control, or rushed passing. Assign if the player dribbles with head down and passes without looking. Use eyes-up dribble work first if the player cannot control the ball; ages 7-8 only with a stationary dribble and short pass.
drills.statistic: The player has to see before making the play. This gives a simple rhythm: control, look, pass.
drills.safety: No speed. Pick the ball up before passing.

drills.name: Two-Cones Receiver Gap
drills.reps_target: reps both sides
drills.instructions: Place two cones a few feet apart as a gap. The receiver starts to one side, steps into the gap, shows hands, catches a soft pass, and secures the ball. The receiver then passes back and exits the gap. Do reps from both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low spacing awareness, poor receiver movement, weak catch readiness, or low passing-window understanding. Assign if the player stands behind imaginary defenders instead of finding open space. Make the gap wider for younger players.
drills.statistic: A receiver can make the pass easier by finding space. This teaches open-window movement without live defense.
drills.safety: Step into the gap. No hard cuts.

drills.name: Pass and Point to Space
drills.reps_target: reps, coach asks "where is space?"
drills.instructions: Pass to a teammate or coach. Right after the pass, point to an open spot on the court where a teammate could move. The coach can ask "where is space?" Point, then reset. Add movement later only if the player understands the idea.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low spacing awareness, poor court vision, weak playmaking IQ, or low team-concept understanding. Assign if the player passes and watches without thinking about the next action. Use coach-guided pointing first if the player cannot identify space.
drills.statistic: Playmaking is not just the pass — it is seeing what happens next. This teaches that idea in a beginner-safe way.
drills.safety: No pressure. Teach the concept slowly.

drills.name: Strong-Hand to Weak-Hand Carry Switch
drills.reps_target: reps, then walk slowly
drills.instructions: Hold the ball on the strong side of the body. Move it across the chest to the weak side, hold for 2 seconds, then move it back. After a few reps, walk slowly while switching. Use a smaller ball if the weak hand struggles.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low weak-hand confidence, poor ball transfer, weak grip, or one-sided ball control. Assign if the player always turns to the strong side or drops the ball when switching hands. Do it standing still before walking.
drills.statistic: Weak-hand play starts with safe ball control. A player does not need advanced dribbles before learning to secure the ball on both sides.
drills.safety: No speed. Keep the ball close to the body.

drills.name: Coach Shows Open Hand Pass
drills.reps_target: reps, switch which target shows hands
drills.instructions: Two coaches or teammates stand close. One shows hands and the other keeps hands down. The passer looks, finds the open hands, and passes softly to that player. The receiver catches and gives the ball back. Switch which target shows hands each rep.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low target recognition, poor decision-making, weak passing accuracy, or high turnover risk. Assign if the player passes to teammates who are not ready. Use one receiver first if two targets are confusing.
drills.statistic: A ready teammate shows a target. This teaches the passer to wait for the cue before making the pass.
drills.safety: No surprise passes. Receivers must be watching.

drills.name: Dribble Around Coach Pass Back
drills.reps_target: reps both directions
drills.instructions: A coach or cone stands still as a marker. Dribble slowly around the marker, gather the ball, and pass back to a receiver behind or beside the starting spot. Start with a wide path and short pass. Do both directions.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low dribble control, weak passing angle, poor gather, or low playmaking awareness. Assign if the player can dribble but cannot pass after changing direction. Use no dribble and walk around the marker first; younger players only with walking speed and the strong hand.
drills.statistic: Players often need to change angle before passing. This keeps the read simple and removes live defense.
drills.safety: No tight turns at speed. Keep the coach out of the path.

drills.name: Short Reversal Pass
drills.reps_target: reps, then reverse direction
drills.instructions: Three players or two players and a coach stand across the top area. The ball starts on one side. Pass to the middle, and the middle passes to the other side. Keep all passes short and controlled. After a few reps, reverse direction. Players call names and show hands.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low ball movement, poor spacing, weak communication, or low team awareness. Assign if the player keeps the ball on one side and does not understand reversing it. Move players closer together for younger athletes.
drills.statistic: Reversing the ball is a simple team playmaking habit. Beginners need short passes and clear spacing before advanced reads.
drills.safety: No long skip passes. Keep distance safe.

drills.name: Receiver Check-In Check-Out
drills.reps_target: reps both wings
drills.instructions: The receiver starts on the wing. Take two steps toward the passer, then two steps back out to open space, show hands, and catch a soft pass. Secure the ball and pass it back. Do both wings.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor receiver timing, low spacing awareness, weak catch readiness, or low off-ball movement. Assign if the player stands still or runs straight into the passer. Walk the movement without the pass first.
drills.statistic: Receivers need to create a passing angle. Checking in and out teaches simple timing before more advanced cuts.
drills.safety: No hard cuts. Move under control.

drills.name: Safe Save Pass
drills.reps_target: reps, slow and close
drills.instructions: A coach rolls or places the ball near a sideline. Step to the ball, secure it with two hands, and make a short safe pass to a nearby teammate or coach — do not jump out of bounds or throw behind the head. Keep it slow and close.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor loose-ball awareness, panic passing, weak ball security, or high turnover risk. Assign if the player saves the ball blindly or throws it to the other team. Remove sideline pressure and do it in open space first; ages 7-8 only with walking speed and no sideline rush.
drills.statistic: Young players often try heroic saves that become turnovers. This teaches secure first, then pass to a teammate.
drills.safety: No diving. No jumping into walls, bleachers, or other players.

drills.name: Seated Soft Catch
drills.reps_target: 8 clean catches, rest, repeat
drills.instructions: Sit on the floor or a stable bench with feet flat. A coach stands close and gives a soft pass to the hands. Catch with two hands, pull the ball to the chest, and say "got it." The coach takes the ball back and repeats. Do 8 clean catches, rest, repeat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low catch confidence, poor soft hands, weak hand strength, or fear of the ball. Assign if the player flinches, turns away, or drops easy passes while standing. Use a foam ball first if the player is scared of the ball.
drills.statistic: Some young athletes need the catching task simplified. Removing movement lets the player focus on tracking, catching, and securing the ball.
drills.safety: Pass softly to the hands. Do not throw near the face.

drills.name: Seated Partner Push Pass
drills.reps_target: reps, slow and controlled
drills.instructions: Two players sit facing each other 4-6 feet apart. Player A pushes the ball softly with two hands to Player B’s hands. Player B catches, secures the ball, and pushes it back. Keep the pass slow and controlled. Use a smaller or lighter ball if needed.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low passing strength, poor aim, weak hand control, or low passing confidence. Assign if the player cannot safely pass while standing yet. Move closer or use a lighter ball if the pass is forced.
drills.statistic: Seated passing is a lower-rung drill that removes running and lower-body timing. It helps younger players build controlled force before standing partner passing.
drills.safety: Keep distance short. No hard throws.

drills.name: Tall-Kneel Catch and Secure
drills.reps_target: 6-8 catches
drills.instructions: Kneel on both knees on a soft surface or court area. A coach stands close and gives a soft pass to the hands. Catch with two hands, pull the ball to the chest, and stay tall without leaning back. The coach takes the ball back and repeats. Do 6-8 catches.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor catch posture, weak core control, low catch security, or low hand confidence. Assign if the player catches while leaning, falling back, or losing posture. Use seated soft catch if kneeling is uncomfortable.
drills.statistic: Kneeling reduces footwork demands but still asks the player to control the upper body. Useful before adding movement.
drills.safety: Do not kneel if the player has knee pain. Use a soft surface if needed.

drills.name: Half-Kneel Target Pass
drills.reps_target: 5 reps, then switch knee down
drills.instructions: Start in a half-kneeling position with one knee down and one foot forward. A partner stands close with target hands. Make a soft two-hand pass to the target, then receive the ball back. Do 5 reps, then switch which knee is down. Keep the distance short.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor trunk control, weak pass accuracy, leaning passes, or low body stability. Assign if the player passes while twisting or falling sideways. Use standing short passes if kneeling bothers the knees.
drills.statistic: Passing accuracy improves when the body stays stable. Half-kneeling teaches control without speed or pressure.
drills.safety: Avoid if knee pain appears. Keep passes soft.

drills.name: Kneel-to-Stand Ball Secure
drills.reps_target: 4 reps leading each leg
drills.instructions: Start in a tall-kneeling position with the ball held strong to the chest. Step one foot forward, stand up slowly, keep the ball secure, then reset. Do 4 reps leading with each leg. Move slowly and keep the ball tight.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low ball security, poor body control, weak grip, or movement-control issues. Assign if the player drops the ball while standing, turning, or changing height. Use a smaller ball or start from seated if kneeling is too hard.
drills.statistic: Ball security should hold up while the body moves. This builds control before faster playmaking movement.
drills.safety: Move slowly. Avoid if knee pain appears.

drills.name: Ball Shelf Walk
drills.reps_target: 2-3 trips
drills.instructions: Hold the ball like it is sitting on a shelf: two hands under and behind the ball, close to the body. Walk 10 steps forward, stop, turn slowly, and walk back. The ball should stay steady. Do 2-3 trips.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low ball security, poor posture, weak hand control, or low confidence carrying the ball. Assign if the player carries the ball loose, swings it, or drops it while walking. Use a smaller ball if the player cannot hold it steady.
drills.statistic: Before passing or dribbling, the player has to carry and control the ball. This builds simple ownership of the ball.
drills.safety: Walk only. Keep the ball below the face.

drills.name: Ball Around Back Hold
drills.reps_target: 5 reps each direction
drills.instructions: Stand still with the ball. Pass the ball behind the back from one hand to the other, then bring it back to the front and hold it at the chest. Start slow. Do 5 reps each direction. This is not a dribble move — the ball stays in the hands.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor hand transfer, low ball awareness, weak coordination, or low body control. Assign if the player loses the ball when moving it behind the body. Use ball carry change hands first if this is too hard.
drills.statistic: Controlled hand transfers support ball security and coordination. Moving behind the body should stay slow and safe for beginners.
drills.safety: No fast behind-the-back dribble. Stop if shoulder pain appears.

drills.name: Low Bounce Catch Control
drills.reps_target: 8-10 clean reps
drills.instructions: Stand with the ball. Give the ball one gentle low bounce, catch it with two hands, and pull it to the chest. The bounce should stay below the waist. Do 8-10 clean reps. Use a smaller ball if needed.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor low-ball control, weak reaction, low hand strength, or fumbled pickups. Assign if the player loses the ball on low bounces or cannot secure it cleanly. Use a softer ball if the bounce is too fast.
drills.statistic: Low ball control is a base skill for playmaking. This builds control without adding dribble speed or defenders.
drills.safety: Keep the bounce low and in front. No chasing wild bounces.

drills.name: Dribble Catch From Coach Roll
drills.reps_target: 6-8 reps
drills.instructions: A coach gently rolls the ball toward the player. Stop the ball with two hands, take 2 slow dribbles, then pick the ball up and secure it at the chest. Give the ball back to the coach and reset. Do 6-8 reps.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor loose-ball control, weak dribble start, low pickup control, or high lost-ball rate. Assign if the player cannot turn a loose ball into controlled possession. Stop and secure the ball only before adding dribbles.
drills.statistic: Games are not always clean catches. This teaches the player to gather a loose ball and turn it into safe control.
drills.safety: No diving. Ball should be rolled slowly.

drills.name: Receiver Stop Sign Hands
drills.reps_target: reps, switch ready signal
drills.instructions: A receiver stands close to the passer. When the receiver shows both hands like a stop sign, the passer gives a soft pass. When the receiver keeps hands down, the passer holds the ball. Switch the ready signal every few reps. Keep it simple and slow.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor receiver readiness, weak visual cues, rushed passing, or low communication. Assign if the passer throws when the teammate is not ready. Use one clear ready signal only for younger players.
drills.statistic: The receiver gives the passer information. This teaches a simple visual cue that helps prevent unsafe passes.
drills.safety: No surprise throws. Pass only when hands are ready.

drills.name: Quiet Catch Challenge
drills.reps_target: 8 clean catches
drills.instructions: A coach gives a soft pass from close range. Catch the ball as quietly as possible, pull it in, and hold it. If the ball makes a loud slap, relax the hands and catch softer. Do 8 clean catches.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor soft hands, low catch control, fumbled catches, or stiff hands. Assign if the ball bounces off the hands or makes loud contact on every catch. Use a softer ball if the player is nervous.
drills.statistic: Soft hands help the player secure the ball instead of knocking it away. This gives an easy sound-based cue.
drills.safety: Use soft passes only. No passes near the face.

drills.name: One-Step Outlet Target
drills.reps_target: reps both sides
drills.instructions: Start near the lane with the ball secured. A receiver stands on the wing. Take one step toward the receiver, keep balance, and pass softly to the target hands. The receiver catches and returns the ball. Do both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor outlet awareness, weak pass accuracy, low balance, or rushed decisions. Assign if the player secures the ball but does not know the safe outlet option. Shorten the pass for younger players.
drills.statistic: A safe outlet pass starts with control and a clear target. This keeps the movement small and the decision simple.
drills.safety: No long passes. Step under control.

drills.name: Receiver Find the Sideline
drills.reps_target: reps both sides
drills.instructions: A passer stands near the middle with the ball. The receiver starts a few steps inside the court. On the coach cue, the receiver moves toward the sideline, shows hands, catches a soft pass, and secures the ball. The receiver passes back and resets. Do both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low spacing awareness, poor receiver movement, weak catch readiness, or low outlet understanding. Assign if the receiver crowds the middle and does not create an outlet angle. Walk the movement without the pass first.
drills.statistic: Receivers create passing lanes by moving to space. The sideline gives a clear visual landmark for beginners.
drills.safety: Stay inbounds and avoid walls or benches.

drills.name: Pass and Freeze Balance
drills.reps_target: 8-10 reps
drills.instructions: Stand close to a partner. Pass softly, then freeze for 2 seconds after the pass. The coach checks if the feet, chest, and head are balanced. The partner passes back, and the player repeats. Do 8-10 reps.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor passing balance, weak body control, low accuracy, or rushed passes. Assign if the player falls forward, twists, or steps wildly after passing. Shorten distance if the player has to throw hard.
drills.statistic: A balanced passer is usually a more accurate passer. Freezing after the pass shows whether the body was under control.
drills.safety: No long passes. Keep the body quiet after release.

drills.name: Two-Hand Tap to Pass
drills.reps_target: 6-8 reps
drills.instructions: Tap the ball lightly between both hands 5 times at chest height. After the fifth tap, catch the ball with two hands and pass softly to a partner. The partner catches and gives the ball back. Do 6-8 reps.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor ball control, weak hand rhythm, low pass readiness, or fumbled passes. Assign if the player can do ball taps but struggles moving into a pass. Do fewer taps or use a smaller ball for younger players.
drills.statistic: Playmaking links ball control and passing. This gives the player a simple rhythm before the pass.
drills.safety: Keep taps below face level. No hard passes.

drills.name: Three-Second Scan Hold
drills.reps_target: reps, no defense first
drills.instructions: Start with the ball secured at the chest. The coach counts to three. During the count, look left, middle, and right while keeping the ball protected. After the count, the coach points to a receiver and the player passes softly. Start with no defense.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor scanning, panic passing, low patience, or weak ball security. Assign if the player catches and throws immediately without looking. Use one receiver first if the player gets overwhelmed.
drills.statistic: Decision-making starts with seeing the floor. A short scan hold builds patience while keeping the ball secure.
drills.safety: No defenders at first. Keep the ball tight.

drills.name: Partner Step-Back Target Catch
drills.reps_target: reps both sides, small step
drills.instructions: A receiver starts close to the passer. Take one controlled step backward, show hands, catch a soft pass, and secure the ball. Pass back and repeat. Work both sides and keep the step small.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low receiver spacing, poor catch balance, weak target hands, or low off-ball awareness. Assign if the receiver crowds the passer or cannot catch after moving back. Use no pass first if stepping back causes balance issues.
drills.statistic: Receivers can make passes easier by creating a little space. This is a safe first spacing movement.
drills.safety: Check space behind the receiver. No fast backpedaling.

drills.name: Safe Middle Pivot Pass
drills.reps_target: reps, switch target each rep
drills.instructions: Start in the middle with the ball. Two receivers stand at short distances, one left and one right. Pivot slowly, look at both targets, and pass to the receiver who shows hands. The receiver catches and returns the ball. Switch target each rep.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor pivot control, low decision-making, weak target recognition, or panic passing. Assign if the player gets the ball in the middle and throws without seeing targets. Use one receiver if two targets are too much.
drills.statistic: The middle of the floor gives options, but beginners can panic there. This makes the decision simple and safe.
drills.safety: Slow pivot only. No defenders or reaching.

drills.name: Calm Corner Hold and Pass
drills.reps_target: reps both corners
drills.instructions: Start in the corner with the ball. Hold the ball strong, take one breath, look at the nearby receiver, and pass softly to the receiver’s hands. The receiver catches and returns the ball. Repeat from both corners. No defender at first.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for corner panic, weak ball security, rushed passing, or high turnover risk. Assign if the player traps themselves in the corner and throws wild passes. Move the receiver closer for younger players.
drills.statistic: The corner is a common beginner turnover spot. This teaches calm, secure, short passing before pressure is added.
drills.safety: No defenders at first. Keep the receiver close.

drills.name: Coach Says Dribble or Pass
drills.reps_target: reps, slow and clear calls
drills.instructions: Start with the ball; a receiver stands close. The coach calls either "dribble" or "pass." On "dribble," take 3 controlled dribbles and secure the ball. On "pass," pass softly to the receiver’s hands. Keep the choices slow and clear.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low listening response, poor decision-making, weak dribble control, or panic with the ball. Assign if the player does not know whether to keep the ball or pass. Use only one command at first if the player gets confused.
drills.statistic: Playmaking starts with simple choices. This teaches the player to hear a cue and make a controlled action without pressure.
drills.safety: No speed. No defenders. Control first.

drills.name: Stance Sit and Stand
drills.reps_target: 6-8 reps
drills.instructions: Stand tall, feet about shoulder-width. On the coach cue, bend the knees, drop the hips slightly, keep the chest up, and hold a defensive stance for 2 seconds. Stand back up and reset. Do 6-8 reps. The stance should be comfortable, not a deep squat.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low stance strength, poor posture, weak balance, or low defensive readiness. Assign if the player stands too upright, bends only at the waist, or cannot hold a safe stance. Shorten the hold if knees, hips, or back feel uncomfortable.
drills.statistic: Younger players often lack the leg strength to hold long defensive stances. Short stance reps teach posture without turning the drill into conditioning.
drills.safety: No deep squat. Stop if knee, hip, or back pain appears.

drills.name: Hands Wide Stance Hold
drills.reps_target: 6-8 reps
drills.instructions: Get into a comfortable defensive stance. Hold both hands wide, palms out, for 3 seconds. The coach checks that the player is not leaning, grabbing, or swiping. Stand up, reset, and repeat. Do 6-8 reps.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor hand activity, low defensive awareness, weak posture, or reaching fouls. Assign if the player keeps hands down or reaches instead of staying balanced. Lower the arms slightly if shoulder fatigue appears.
drills.statistic: Early defensive development should teach safe positioning before pressure. Wide hands help players contest space without fouling.
drills.safety: No grabbing or swiping. Stop if shoulder pain appears.

drills.name: Mirror Stance Partner
drills.reps_target: 10s, rest, switch roles
drills.instructions: Two players face each other with no ball. Player A leads, slowly moving the hands, shoulders, or body side to side. Player B mirrors the movement while staying in a comfortable stance. Go for 10 seconds, rest, switch roles. Keep it slow.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor reaction control, weak stance balance, low focus, or poor body control. Assign if the player loses stance when watching another person. Use hand-only mirroring for younger players.
drills.statistic: Defenders need to react without jumping out of position. Mirroring gives a safe reaction task before live offense is added.
drills.safety: No contact, no fast cuts, no chasing.

drills.name: Slide Two Steps and Freeze
drills.reps_target: 6 reps each direction
drills.instructions: Start in a comfortable stance. On the coach cue, slide two short steps to the right and freeze. Then slide two short steps to the left and freeze. The coach checks feet, knees, and balance. Do 6 reps each direction.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor lateral control, weak footwork, low balance, or crossed feet. Assign if the player crosses feet, hops, or loses balance during slides. Use one step each way for younger players or low-strength athletes.
drills.statistic: Defensive sliding should start with short controlled steps. Beginners need control before speed or longer slide patterns.
drills.safety: Short steps only. Stop if ankle or knee pain appears.

drills.name: Angle Cut-Off Walk
drills.reps_target: reps, switch roles
drills.instructions: Place two cones in a lane. The offensive player walks from one cone toward the other without a ball. The defender starts beside them and walks to cut off the path, staying between the player and the basket. No contact. Switch roles after each rep.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor defensive angle, low positioning awareness, weak body control, or chasing habits. Assign if the player follows behind the offense instead of getting in front. Use slower walking speed if the defender gets confused; ages 7-8 do it as a walking game.
drills.statistic: Good defense starts with position. Walking angle work teaches the idea before speed, contact, or live dribbling is added.
drills.safety: No bumping or blocking. Walk only.

drills.name: Ball-Side Point Drill
drills.reps_target: reps, add "basket" point if ready
drills.instructions: A coach stands with a ball on one side of the court; the player stands in the middle. The coach moves the ball to different spots. The player points to the ball and says "ball," then resets into a comfortable stance. Add "basket" as a second point if the player is ready.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low ball awareness, poor defensive focus, weak court understanding, or low help-side readiness. Assign if the player loses track of the ball on defense. Use one ball spot at a time for younger players.
drills.statistic: Players cannot defend or rebound well if they do not know where the ball is. A low-load awareness drill.
drills.safety: No running. Teach the concept first.

drills.name: Ball-You-Man Triangle
drills.reps_target: reps, walking pace
drills.instructions: Use three people: coach with the ball, defender, and offensive player. The defender stands where they can see both the ball and the offensive player. The coach moves the ball slowly to a new spot, and the defender adjusts — pointing one hand toward the ball and one toward their player.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low off-ball awareness, poor help positioning, weak visual tracking, or poor defensive spacing. Assign if the player watches only the ball and loses their matchup. Use walking pace and clear spacing only.
drills.statistic: Off-ball defense starts with vision. This teaches the relationship between the ball, the defender, and the matchup.
drills.safety: No live cuts or screens. Walk and point.

drills.name: Closeout Hands High Stop
drills.reps_target: 6 reps
drills.instructions: Start 6-8 feet from a coach holding the ball. Take quick but controlled steps toward the coach, slow down, raise both hands, and stop balanced. Do not jump, swipe, or crowd the coach. Reset and repeat 6 reps.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor closeout control, weak stop balance, low hand activity, or fly-by risk. Assign if the player runs past the shooter or closes out with hands down. Walk the closeout if stopping control is poor; ages 7-8 only with walking closeouts.
drills.statistic: Closeouts are common in youth defense, but speed must be controlled. Beginners need to learn slow-down and hands-up before live contests.
drills.safety: No contact with the shooter. No jumping into the coach.

drills.name: Contest Without Jump
drills.reps_target: reps, add soft shot only if safe
drills.instructions: A coach or partner holds the ball in shooting position. The defender stands a safe distance away, gets into stance, raises one or both hands, and holds the contest for 2 seconds — staying on the floor. Reset and repeat. Add a soft shot only if the player can keep space safely.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor contest control, high foul risk, low discipline, or weak defensive hand position. Assign if the player jumps into shooters, reaches, or cannot contest without fouling. Use no shot attempt at first.
drills.statistic: Beginners often foul because they jump or swipe. This teaches a low-risk contest with hands high and feet down.
drills.safety: Stay on the floor. Keep safe distance from the shooter.

drills.name: No-Ball Box-Out Turn
drills.reps_target: reps both sides
drills.instructions: A coach points to an imaginary shooter. The player says "shot," turns to find the nearest partner or cone, steps into a safe box-out position, and holds for 2 seconds. No pushing and no ball. Reset and repeat from both sides.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor box-out awareness, weak footwork, low rebounding positioning, or low possession awareness. Assign if the player watches the ball and forgets to find their player after a shot. Use a cone instead of a player for younger athletes.
drills.statistic: Youth drills often start box-out work without a ball so players learn the movement first, reducing contact and confusion.
drills.safety: No pushing. Hold space, do not hit the partner.

drills.name: Box-Out Back-to-Contact Hold
drills.reps_target: 5 reps, then switch roles
drills.instructions: A defender stands in front of a partner. On the coach cue, the defender turns, places their back lightly against the partner’s front, keeps arms safe, and holds position for 2 seconds. The partner gives only light resistance. No ball is used. Switch roles after 5 reps.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for low contact confidence, poor box-out balance, weak body control, or fear of rebounding contact. Assign if the player avoids contact completely but has safe movement control. Avoid for players with fear of contact, pain, or poor balance; younger players should use cone box-outs instead.
drills.statistic: Rebounding has contact, but it must be introduced carefully. Light contact holds are safer than competitive rebounding for beginners.
drills.safety: Light contact only. No pushing, leaning hard, elbows, or wrestling.

drills.name: Shot Call Find Player
drills.reps_target: reps, turn both ways
drills.instructions: Players stand in pairs. The coach calls "shot." Each defender turns to find their partner, gets into a safe box-out position, and holds for 2 seconds. No ball needed at first. After a few reps, the coach points to different directions so players learn to turn both ways.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor rebounding awareness, weak box-out reaction, low player-location skill, or low possession finish habits. Assign if the player ball-watches after shots and gives up rebounds. Use cones for younger players who are not ready for body contact.
drills.statistic: A key rebounding habit is "shot, find, hit, get." For beginners, this starts with the "find" piece before adding contact or ball pursuit.
drills.safety: No bumping. Find and hold only.

drills.name: Two-Hand Rebound Catch
drills.reps_target: 6-8 clean rebounds
drills.instructions: A coach stands close and tosses the ball softly off the backboard or straight up. Track it, catch with two hands, land balanced, and pull the ball to the chest or chin. Start with low tosses. Do 6-8 clean rebounds.
drills.coaching_notes: Best for poor rebound catching, weak hands, low tracking, or loose rebound security. Assign if the player bats at rebounds or catches with one hand only. Use no-jump catches for younger or low-strength players.
drills.statistic: Rebounding is not finished until the ball is secured. Two-hand catches build control and reduce loose-ball rebounds.
drills.safety: Use low tosses. Land balanced. No crowding under the ball.

drills.name: Rebound Chin and Outlet
drills.reps_target: reps both sides
drills.instructions: A coach tosses the ball softly to the player or off the backboard. Catch with two hands, bring the ball to the chin or chest, pivot slowly, and make a short outlet pass to a coach or teammate. Keep the outlet close and controlled. Do both sides.
